sections.heading: Statutory Notice
sections.text: A landlord must give a tenant who defaults on any lease term a ten-day statutory notice to quit before commencing an unlawful detainer action. Ala. Code § 35-9-6.

sections.heading: Self-Help / Commercial Lockout
sections.text: Self-help remedies (lockouts, seizure of premises without judicial process) remain unavailable in Alabama. Ala. Code § 6-6-317.

sections.heading: Jurisdiction and Venue
sections.text: District and circuit courts have jurisdiction over eviction actions according to their respective statutory jurisdictional amounts, and venue lies in the county where the leased property is located. Ala. Code § 35-9A-461(b). District courts retain a $20,000 damages jurisdictional limit, Ala. Code § 12-11-30(1), so a commercial landlord seeking damages beyond that amount must pursue a separate or supplemental claim in circuit court (including on appeal).

sections.heading: Timing
sections.text: After the notice period expires, the landlord serves a summons and complaint. Ala. Code § 35-9-6. A tenant has 14 days to respond for nonpayment of rent and 7 days to respond for other grounds; the tenant then has 7 days to appeal an adverse ruling, after which the landlord may obtain a writ of possession. Ala. Code § 35-9A-461(d). Eviction actions receive scheduling precedence over other civil cases, and on appeal to circuit court the case is set for trial within 60 days of the appeal filing. Ala. Code § 6-6-350.

sections.heading: Damages
sections.text: Eviction and repossession generally terminate the lease and the landlord's right to post-eviction rent, but the parties may contract to hold the tenant liable for rent accruing after eviction, and Alabama courts enforce express acceleration clauses. Landlords have no statutory duty to mitigate damages. A tenant who unlawfully holds over after lease expiration may be liable for double rent. Ala. Code § 6-6-314.

sections.heading: Special Considerations
sections.text: An appeal from a district court eviction judgment must be filed within seven days and is entitled to preferred trial scheduling in circuit court, but a tenant's appeal does not stay the writ of possession unless the tenant pays into court all rent due under the lease and continues paying rent as it accrues during the appeal. Ala. Code §§ 6-6-350, 35-9A-461(d).

leaseConsiderations: Express acceleration-of-rent clause, since Alabama will not imply one.
Express post-eviction/post-repossession rent liability language, since termination otherwise cuts off future rent.
No reliance on self-help; build in judicial-process timelines for default scenarios.
Contractual notice/cure periods tailored to the tenant's typical default patterns (statute sets only a 10-day floor).
Anticipate a bifurcated forum: possession in district court capped at $20,000, larger damages claims in circuit court.
Double-rent holdover language to reinforce the statutory holdover remedy.
Attorney's fees provision, since fee-shifting is not automatic.
Appeal-bond/rent-deposit mechanics to preserve possession pending a tenant's appeal.
sourceNotes:
Statutory authorities reviewed: Ala. Code §§ 35-9-6, 35-9A-461(b), (d), 12-11-30(1), 6-6-317, 6-6-314, 6-6-350. No material 2023–2026 amendments to these commercial eviction provisions were identified; citations and substance were confirmed against current Alabama Code text.

sections.heading: Statutory Notice
sections.text: A landlord must give the tenant written notice to quit before commencing an action to recover possession. Alaska Stat. § 34.03.220(b). For nonpayment of rent, the landlord may proceed after 7 days' notice; for non-monetary lease violations, a 10-day notice is required. Alaska Stat. §§ 34.03.220(b), 09.45.090(b)(2)(A). Notice may be delivered personally, left at the premises, or sent by registered or certified mail, and 3 days are added to the notice period when service is by mail. Alaska Stat. §§ 09.45.100, 09.45.090(c).

sections.heading: Self-Help / Commercial Lockout
sections.text: Where the lease so provides, a landlord may re-enter for nonpayment of rent, but any self-help re-entry must be peaceable. Alaska Stat. §§ 09.45.690, 09.45.060. A landlord may not seize a tenant's property to satisfy rent. Alaska Stat. § 34.03.250.

sections.heading: Jurisdiction and Venue
sections.text: Possession is recovered through an unlawful detainer action. Alaska Stat. § 09.45.070. District court has jurisdiction where arrears and property damage do not exceed $100,000; larger claims proceed in superior court. Alaska Stat. §§ 22.15.030(a)(6), (b), 22.10.020.

sections.heading: Timing
sections.text: A possession hearing is typically set within about two weeks of filing; damages claims proceed in the ordinary course of litigation and do not receive priority docketing.

sections.heading: Damages
sections.text: Acceleration-of-rent clauses are enforceable where expressly provided; absent such a clause, a landlord should mitigate by seeking a replacement tenant. A tenant who pays all arrears, interest, and costs before judgment and cures other lease breaches may be entitled to continue in possession unless the lease provides otherwise. Alaska Stat. § 09.45.690.

leaseConsiderations: Express, unambiguous re-entry/self-help clause if the landlord wants to preserve that remedy — it is contract-dependent, not automatic.
Reinforce that any self-help must remain peaceable to avoid tort exposure.
Express acceleration clause, since none is implied.
Mitigation language allocating responsibility for reletting efforts.
Address the statutory reinstatement right (payment of arrears cures default) if the landlord wants to limit or condition it contractually.
Specify notice delivery method in the lease to avoid the statutory 3-day mail extension where speed matters.
Distinguish monetary (7-day) vs. non-monetary (10-day) default notice triggers in default provisions.
Anticipate venue/forum depending on claim size ($100,000 threshold between district and superior court).
sourceNotes:
Statutory authorities reviewed: Alaska Stat. §§ 34.03.220(b), 34.03.250, 09.45.060, 09.45.070, 09.45.090(b)(2)(A), (c), 09.45.100, 09.45.690, 22.10.020, 22.15.030(a)(6), (b). No material 2023–2026 legislative amendments specific to commercial forcible entry and detainer or the Alaska Landlord and Tenant Act's commercial provisions were identified in current searches.

sections.heading: Statutory Notice
sections.text: A landlord must give a written demand to quit and wait five days before pursuing self-help or a forcible detainer action. Ariz. Rev. Stat. § 12-1173(2).

sections.heading: Self-Help / Commercial Lockout
sections.text: Arizona continues to permit commercial self-help. Where a tenant fails to pay rent for five days, the landlord may re-enter and take possession without further formal demand. Ariz. Rev. Stat. § 33-361(A). If rent remains unpaid, the landlord also holds a statutory lien and may seize as much of the tenant's on-premises personal property as necessary to secure the rent, subject to procedural requirements (notice periods and, ultimately, a public sale) and the exclusion of property belonging to third parties or otherwise exempt by law. Ariz. Rev. Stat. § 33-361(D); see also Ariz. Rev. Stat. § 33-1023 (sale procedure). Separately, a landlord may pursue prejudgment attachment of a tenant's assets for lease breaches under Ariz. Rev. Stat. § 12-2401 et seq.

sections.heading: Jurisdiction and Venue
sections.text: The court in a forcible detainer action may determine possession and simultaneously assess damages, attorney's fees, and costs, or the landlord may bring a separate action for unpaid rent and damages. Ariz. Rev. Stat. § 33-361(B). Justice courts have concurrent jurisdiction with superior court for amounts of $10,000 or less, Ariz. Rev. Stat. § 22-201(C), while superior court has jurisdiction over forcible entry and detainer actions regardless of amount. Ariz. Const. art. VI, § 14(5).

sections.heading: Timing
sections.text: A forcible entry and detainer action must be tried not less than five nor more than thirty days after commencement. Ariz. Rev. Stat. § 33-361. No writ of restitution issues until five days after judgment, but once issued it is enforced promptly. Ariz. Rev. Stat. § 12-1178(C).

sections.heading: Damages
sections.text: Courts may award all charges due under the rental agreement plus damages, attorney's fees, and costs. An acceleration clause must be express to be enforceable, and landlords have no duty to mitigate. Ariz. Rev. Stat. § 33-361(D).

sections.heading: Special Considerations
sections.text: Any party may appeal within five days of judgment, but must pay into court the rent due and continue paying rent as it accrues during the appeal. Ariz. Rev. Stat. § 12-1179(A), (D). Separately, effective 2026, S.B. 1426 amended Ariz. Rev. Stat. §§ 12-1171 and 12-1173 to create an expedited forcible detainer track for removing unauthorized occupants ("squatters") who never had a landlord-tenant relationship; the bill expressly does not alter existing landlord-tenant rights and remedies and does not apply to current or former tenants, so it has no effect on standard commercial lease enforcement.

leaseConsiderations: Express lockout/self-help procedures consistent with § 33-361(A) to preserve the landlord's non-judicial remedy.
Landlord's lien and property-seizure mechanics referenced or clarified in the default section.
Express acceleration clause, since none is implied.
No mitigation obligation by default — consider whether to impose one contractually.
Attorney's fees and costs provision to support fee recovery alongside possession.
Consider whether to reserve the right to a separate damages action versus combining claims in the forcible detainer proceeding.
Appeal bond/rent-deposit provisions consistent with the five-day appeal window.
Confirm tenant status is unambiguous in the lease, since squatter-focused expedited procedures under S.B. 1426 are unavailable against actual tenants.
sourceNotes:
Statutory authorities reviewed: Ariz. Rev. Stat. §§ 12-1173(2), 12-1178(C), 12-1179(A), (D), 12-2401 et seq., 22-201(C), 33-361(A), (B), (D), 33-1023; Ariz. Const. art. VI, § 14(5); S.B. 1426 (2026), amending Ariz. Rev. Stat. §§ 12-1171, 12-1173, effective 2026 (expedited unauthorized-occupant procedure; does not alter landlord-tenant remedies).

sections.heading: Statutory Notice
sections.text: A landlord must give the tenant a ten-day notice to quit. Ark. Code Ann. § 18-16-101(b)(1).

sections.heading: Self-Help / Commercial Lockout
sections.text: Self-help is not available in Arkansas. Ark. Code Ann. § 18-60-302.

sections.heading: Jurisdiction and Venue
sections.text: A landlord may seek both possession and damages in the same unlawful detainer proceeding, filed in circuit court in the county where the property is located. Ark. Code Ann. § 18-60-306.

sections.heading: Timing
sections.text: If the tenant does not file a written objection to the claim for possession within five days after service of the complaint, the clerk must immediately issue a writ of possession without delay. Ark. Code Ann. § 18-60-307(b).

sections.heading: Damages
sections.text: Upon judgment for the landlord, the court assesses rent due through judgment, and if the tenant remains in possession more than 24 hours after service of a writ of possession, the court may order the tenant's possessions applied to satisfy any money judgment. Ark. Code Ann. § 18-60-310(c)(1), (3). Where the property is used for commercial (or mixed residential/commercial) purposes, the landlord is entitled to liquidated damages of three times the monthly rental value for the period of unlawful detention. Ark. Code Ann. § 18-60-309(b)(2). Arkansas imposes no express statutory duty to mitigate.

sections.heading: Special Considerations
sections.text: If the lease provides for acceleration of rent or termination of possession without termination of the lease itself, the landlord may pursue rent through the end of the lease term following eviction.

leaseConsiderations: Express acceleration clause and/or "termination of possession without termination of lease" language to preserve post-eviction rent claims.
No statutory mitigation duty — consider whether to impose one, since courts may otherwise decline to require it.
Combined possession-and-damages pleading is available in a single circuit court action — align lease remedies provisions accordingly.
Contractual notice periods, since the ten-day statutory notice is a floor that parties may lengthen (but should not shorten below the statute).
Reinforce the triple-rent commercial holdover remedy in default/holdover provisions to make tenants aware of the enhanced exposure.
Attorney's fees provision, since fee-shifting is not automatic under these sections.
Provisions addressing disposition of tenant property left behind after a writ of possession is executed.
sourceNotes:
Statutory authorities reviewed: Ark. Code Ann. §§ 18-16-101(b)(1), 18-60-302, 18-60-306, 18-60-307(b), 18-60-309(a), (b)(2), 18-60-310(c)(1), (3). No material 2023–2026 amendments to Arkansas's unlawful detainer statutes affecting commercial tenancies were identified.

classificationNote: Self-help remains categorically unavailable, but the 2026 procedural amendments meaningfully shorten the timeline for landlords facing dilatory motion practice, offsetting some of the friction of the unlawful detainer process.

sections.heading: Statutory Notice
sections.text: Commercial notice requirements depend upon the basis for termination and the provisions of the lease. Before initiating an unlawful detainer action, landlords should verify the applicable commercial notice provisions, cure rights, and lease-specific requirements governing the default at issue. Current notice analysis should always be reviewed in conjunction with California's unlawful detainer statutes and the lease language.

sections.heading: Self-Help / Commercial Lockout
sections.text: Self-help is not an available commercial eviction remedy in California. Commercial landlords generally must recover possession through unlawful detainer proceedings rather than lockout or other unilateral exclusion methods.

sections.heading: Jurisdiction and Venue
sections.text: Commercial possession disputes are generally resolved through unlawful detainer proceedings in superior court. Because the scope of relief available in an unlawful detainer action is narrower than in general civil litigation, landlords should separately evaluate possession claims and broader lease-damage claims. Depending on the circumstances, additional lease-damage claims may require separate litigation.

sections.heading: Timing
sections.text: California continues to provide expedited unlawful detainer procedures. Effective January 1, 2026, Assembly Bill 1384 amended Code of Civil Procedure § 1170. In a commercial unlawful detainer action, when a defendant files a demurrer or motion to strike, the hearing generally must occur between five and seven court days after filing. In commercial tenancy cases, any continuance granted for good cause may not exceed ten court days after the first hearing date established by the court. These amendments were enacted to reduce delays in commercial unlawful detainer proceedings.

sections.heading: Damages
sections.text: California Civil Code § 1951.2 governs damages following termination of a lease due to tenant breach. Upon termination, a landlord may recover unpaid rent earned before termination; rent damages accruing through the time of award; future-rent damages where authorized by the lease and statute; and other detriment proximately caused by the tenant's breach. Future-rent recovery remains subject to the requirements of Civil Code § 1951.2(c), and mitigation principles continue to apply. A landlord's efforts to mitigate damages do not waive the right to recover damages authorized by § 1951.2.

sections.heading: Mitigation
sections.text: California continues to reduce recoverable post-termination and future-rent damages by rental losses that could reasonably have been avoided. The statutory framework expressly contemplates mitigation while preserving the landlord's damages claims.

sections.heading: 2026 Update Note
sections.text: Effective January 1, 2026, AB 1384 amended California Code of Civil Procedure § 1170 and imposed stricter timing requirements for hearings on demurrers and motions to strike in commercial unlawful detainer proceedings. Commercial landlords should evaluate pleading strategy and motion practice with these expedited hearing requirements in mind.

leaseConsiderations: Express future-rent damages provision.
Acceleration clause complying with Civil Code § 1951.2.
Attorney's fees provision.
Detailed default and cure provisions.
Reservation of remedies following reentry.
Non-waiver language for acceptance of payments.
Clarification of mitigation and reletting rights.
Post-termination damage provisions.
sourceNotes: Statutory authorities reviewed: California Code of Civil Procedure § 1170 as amended by Assembly Bill 1384, Chapter 299, Statutes of 2025, effective January 1, 2026; California Civil Code § 1951.2.

sections.heading: Statutory Notice
sections.text: Colorado requires at least three days' written notice after a tenant's default before an eviction action may proceed; a lease may require earlier notice but may not waive the three-day minimum. Colo. Rev. Stat. § 13-40-104 (unlawful detention; formerly cited by some sources as Title 12, now codified in Title 13's Forcible Entry and Detainer article).

sections.heading: Self-Help / Commercial Lockout
sections.text: Colorado prohibits self-help exclusion or removal of a tenant except by mutual consent or where the unit has been abandoned. Colo. Rev. Stat. § 38-12-510.

sections.heading: Jurisdiction and Venue
sections.text: Possession actions may be filed in county or district court in the county where the property is located; claims involving monthly rent exceeding $25,000 must be certified to district court, and county courts otherwise have jurisdiction over rent/damages claims and counterclaims up to $25,000 (exclusive of costs and fees). Colo. Rev. Stat. § 13-40-109. Damages and possession claims must be filed separately.

sections.heading: Timing
sections.text: If a tenant fails to comply with a written demand for compliance or possession, the court issues a summons for a hearing set between seven and fourteen days after issuance.

sections.heading: Damages
sections.text: A landlord may recover the difference between the rent reserved under the lease and the reasonable rental value of the premises for the balance of the term, plus consequential damages, provided the landlord fulfills its duty to mitigate.

sections.heading: Special Considerations
sections.text: Colorado enacted significant tenant-protection legislation in 2024–2026 — including H.B. 24-1098 (requiring "cause" for eviction of a residential tenant, effective April 19, 2024) and H.B. 25-1168 (housing protections and rent-repayment-plan requirements for victim-survivors of domestic violence and related abuse, effective August 6, 2025) — but both measures are expressly limited to residential tenancies and dwelling units and do not alter the commercial forcible entry and detainer framework described above.

leaseConsiderations: Contractual notice periods may exceed but not shorten the three-day statutory minimum.
No self-help — build default enforcement around judicial process and abandonment/mutual-consent exceptions.
Express mitigation-of-damages language, since Colorado imposes a duty to mitigate as a matter of law.
Plan for separately filed possession and damages actions, and address venue if monthly rent may exceed $25,000.
Liquidated/acceleration damages provisions tied to the "loss of bargain" measure (contract rent less reasonable rental value) to reduce proof burdens at trial.
Attorney's fees and cost-shifting provisions, since none is implied.

Confirm the tenancy is genuinely commercial in the lease recitals, since recent residential-only reforms (just-cause eviction, victim-survivor protections) create risk if a mixed-use classification is contested.
sourceNotes:
Statutory authorities reviewed: Colo. Rev. Stat. §§ 13-40-104, 13-40-109, 38-12-510; H.B. 24-1098 (2024), effective April 19, 2024 (residential just-cause eviction; does not apply to commercial tenancies); H.B. 25-1168 (2025), effective August 6, 2025 (residential victim-survivor housing protections; does not apply to commercial tenancies).

sections.heading: Statutory Notice
sections.text: Where a commercial tenant defaults on rent or breaches the lease, the landlord must give three days' notice to quit before terminating the rental agreement or the time specified for the tenant to quit possession. Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-23. If the tenant remains after the notice period, a court commissioner may issue a writ, summons, and complaint. Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-23a. If the tenant's whereabouts are unknown, notice by publication (at least twice, at least ten days before the quit date) suffices. Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-23b. Connecticut also maintains a separate provision specifically addressing eviction of tenants and occupants from commercial property and disposition of property left behind. Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-42a.

sections.heading: Self-Help / Commercial Lockout
sections.text: Self-help methods such as lockouts remain unavailable to Connecticut commercial landlords. Connecticut's entry and detainer statute makes it unlawful for a landlord to retake possession from a tenant holding over by force or a breach of the peace, and a landlord has no right to regain possession from a tenant by self-help even where the tenant is unlawfully holding over. Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-43 (Chapter 833, Entry and Detainer).

sections.heading: Jurisdiction and Venue
sections.text: Summary process actions must be brought in the geographical judicial district where the premises are located, or, for a corporate defendant, where it maintains an office or place of business; if the defendant is a nonresident, venue lies where the plaintiff resides or where the land lies, at the plaintiff's election. Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-23a.

sections.heading: Timing
sections.text: If the tenant has not vacated by the date specified in the notice to quit, the landlord may have a summons and complaint served. The defendant has two days after the return date to appear; absent an appearance by the third day after the return date, the landlord may move for default judgment.

sections.heading: Damages
sections.text: A landlord who terminates a commercial tenancy following the tenant's breach has a duty to mitigate and cannot also recover rent due under the full lease term; but a landlord who declines to accept surrender and instead sues for rent as it comes due (without terminating the tenancy) has no duty to mitigate.

sections.heading: Special Considerations
sections.text: Connecticut adopted eviction-record-sealing legislation in 2024 (limiting public access to certain dismissed/withdrawn/tenant-prevailing eviction case records) and expanded "just cause"/good-cause protections for specified residential tenant categories effective October 1, 2024; both measures are residential-focused and do not extend good-cause eviction protections to commercial tenancies. A broader residential "just cause" bill (S.B. 143, 2024) was not enacted.

leaseConsiderations: Express notice-and-cure provisions, since the statutory three-day quit notice is a floor.
No self-help — rely on judicial summary process for all removals.

Mitigation-of-damages strategy: consider a "no-termination, sue-as-rent-comes-due" remedies clause to preserve full lease-term rent recovery without a mitigation duty, alongside a standard termination-and-relet remedy.
Venue provisions consistent with the judicial-district rules, particularly for out-of-state corporate or nonresident tenants.
Attorney's fees provision, since fee-shifting is not automatic.
Address disposition of tenant property left on commercial premises post-eviction, referencing § 47a-42a.
Default/appearance timeline awareness (two-day appearance window) when drafting notice/cure mechanics that anticipate litigation speed.
sourceNotes:
Statutory authorities reviewed: Conn. Gen. Stat. §§ 47a-23, 47a-23a, 47a-23b, 47a-42a, Chapter 832 generally. 2024 Connecticut legislation on eviction-record sealing and expanded good-cause protections for certain residential tenant categories (effective October 1, 2024) reviewed and confirmed inapplicable to commercial tenancies; S.B. 143 (2024 broader just-cause bill) was not enacted.

sections.heading: Statutory Notice
sections.text: Commercial rental units are expressly excluded from Delaware's Residential Landlord-Tenant Code; all rights, remedies, and obligations under a commercial rental agreement are governed by general contract principles, and only Chapter 57 (Summary Possession) and Part IV of Title 25 apply to commercial rental agreements. Del. Code Ann. tit. 25, § 5101(b). A summary possession action may proceed on grounds including those set by the commercial rental agreement itself. Del. Code Ann. tit. 25, § 5702(10). Notice of the summary possession complaint must be served at least five days and not more than thirty days before the hearing. Del. Code Ann. tit. 25, § 5705.

sections.heading: Self-Help / Commercial Lockout
sections.text: Delaware does not recognize self-help as an available commercial eviction remedy; recovery of possession from a commercial tenant must proceed through the Chapter 57 summary possession action.

sections.heading: Jurisdiction and Venue
sections.text: Summary possession actions are heard by the Justice of the Peace Court in the county where the premises are located. Del. Code Ann. tit. 25, § 5701.

sections.heading: Timing
sections.text: The action commences by filing a complaint for possession; hearing timing follows the notice window in § 5705 and is otherwise court-dependent. Del. Code Ann. tit. 25, § 5704.

sections.heading: Damages
sections.text: Upon judgment for the landlord, the court awards costs to the prevailing party, and for claims based on forcible entry or forcible holding out, the court may award a fixed sum as damages in addition to costs. Del. Code Ann. tit. 25, § 5711. An acceleration clause must be expressly stated to be enforceable, and because commercial tenancies are governed by contract principles, the lease itself must specify whether the landlord may collect rent as contract damages after eviction. Delaware law imposes a duty to mitigate damages.

sections.heading: Special Considerations
sections.text: Because commercial tenancies sit outside the Residential Landlord-Tenant Code, drafters cannot rely on Code default rules to fill lease gaps — the written lease effectively is the governing law on notice, cure, damages, and remedies, subject only to the Chapter 57 court procedure.

leaseConsiderations: Comprehensive, self-contained default/notice/cure provisions — Delaware's contract-principles approach means gaps are not filled by residential-code protections.
Express acceleration-of-rent and post-eviction damages clauses, since none is implied.
Mitigation language, since Delaware imposes a duty to mitigate as a matter of law.
No self-help remedy — build enforcement around the Chapter 57 Justice of the Peace Court process.
Attorney's fees and cost-shifting provisions.
Confirm the "commercial rental unit" characterization is unambiguous in the lease to avoid inadvertent application of residential-code provisions.
Notice timing consistent with the 5–30 day window under § 5705 for any summary possession filing.
sourceNotes:
Statutory authorities reviewed: Del. Code Ann. tit. 25, §§ 5101(b), 5701, 5702(10), 5704, 5705, 5711. Delaware's 2024 residential eviction diversion program (§ 5702A, mandatory mediation for residential filings on/after July 1, 2024) was reviewed and confirmed to apply only to residential summary possession filings, not commercial.

sections.heading: Statutory Notice
sections.text: A commercial month-to-month or quarter-to-quarter tenancy may be terminated by 30 days' written notice from the landlord to the tenant to quit (by contrast, only the tenant — not the landlord — may unilaterally terminate a residential month-to-month tenancy under this section), with the notice period expiring on the first day of the first month at least 30 days after the date of the notice. D.C. Code § 42-3202. The parties may agree to a longer or shorter notice period, or waive the notice requirement, in the lease. D.C. Code § 42-3208.

sections.heading: Self-Help / Commercial Lockout
sections.text: Self-help is not available in the District of Columbia.

sections.heading: Jurisdiction and Venue
sections.text: An action for possession may be filed in the Superior Court of the District of Columbia, and the landlord may seek rent in arrears together with possession, or file separate suits for possession and damages, which may be consolidated.

sections.heading: Timing
sections.text: Timing is variable and case-dependent; there is no fixed statutory hearing window generally applicable to commercial possession actions.

sections.heading: Damages
sections.text: Eviction generally terminates the lease and the tenant's ongoing rent obligation, so statutory provisions typically speak to rent in arrears rather than future rent; however, case law permits a landlord to seek damages for loss of rent measured by the lease terms in appropriate circumstances.

sections.heading: 2026 Update Note
sections.text: Effective December 31, 2025, the Rebalancing Expectations for Neighbors, Tenants, and Landlords (RENTAL) Amendment Act of 2025, D.C. Law 26-80, made substantial changes to D.C.'s eviction framework — including expedited proceedings for dangerous-crime cases, a reduced pre-filing notice period (from 30 to 10 days) for residential nonpayment cases, and new ERAP-stay procedures under D.C. Code § 42-3505.01(r). These changes are limited to residential rental housing (rental units, housing accommodations, dwelling units) under the Rental Housing Act framework and do not apply to commercial tenancies, which continue to be governed by D.C. Code § 42-3202 and related general landlord-tenant provisions described above.

leaseConsiderations: Express notice-period provisions, since the 30-day default notice may be shortened, lengthened, or waived by agreement.
No self-help — enforcement must proceed through Superior Court.
Decide whether to combine possession and damages claims or reserve damages for a separate (potentially consolidated) suit.
Express post-eviction/future-rent damages clause, since termination otherwise cuts off the landlord's rent claim absent contractual or case-law support.
Attorney's fees provision, since fee-shifting is not automatic.
Confirm the lease is unambiguously commercial, since the RENTAL Act's 2025 reforms materially tightened residential eviction timing and protections — misclassification risk has increased.
Build in realistic timing expectations, since commercial possession timing in D.C. remains variable and court-dependent.
sourceNotes:
Statutory authorities reviewed: D.C. Code §§ 42-3202, 42-3208, 42-3505.01(r); RENTAL Amendment Act of 2025, D.C. Law 26-80, effective December 31, 2025 (residential-only reforms).

sections.heading: Statutory Notice
sections.text: A landlord must give three days' written notice requiring payment of rent or possession for a monetary default. Fla. Stat. § 83.20(2). For a non-monetary material breach (where the lease is silent or the tenancy is oral), the landlord must give 15 days' written notice to cure or vacate. Fla. Stat. § 83.20(3). Both the statutory cure periods and notice requirements may be waived by agreement.

sections.heading: Self-Help / Commercial Lockout
sections.text: Self-help is not permitted in Florida; a landlord may obtain possession only through an action at law. Fla. Stat. §§ 83.05, 83.21.

sections.heading: Jurisdiction and Venue
sections.text: A complaint to remove a commercial tenant is filed in the court of the county where the premises are situated. Fla. Stat. § 83.21.

sections.heading: Timing
sections.text: A landlord must serve a summons and complaint at least five days before a judgment for final removal is entered. Fla. Stat. § 83.22. Timing thereafter is variable depending on whether the matter is contested; in a contested nonpayment case, the tenant must deposit the accrued rent into the court registry or move the court to determine the amount to be deposited as a condition of contesting.

sections.heading: Damages
sections.text: A landlord may combine a claim for money damages with a possession claim if pleaded "expressly and specifically," and may also recover attorney's fees and costs. Fla. Stat. §§ 83.231, 83.251. A tenant who refuses to deliver possession after lease expiration may be liable for double rent for the holdover period, plus interest. Fla. Stat. § 83.06. Florida landlords have a duty to mitigate damages, and Florida courts enforce express rent-acceleration clauses.

leaseConsiderations: Express acceleration clause, since Florida courts require one to enforce accelerated rent.
Mitigation-of-damages allocation, since Florida imposes a mitigation duty as a matter of law.
Combine possession and damages claims expressly in remedies language to preserve the option under §§ 83.231/83.251.
Attorney's fees provision to support fee recovery alongside a Chapter 83, Part I action.
Double-rent holdover clause reinforcing the statutory § 83.06 remedy.
Consider whether to shorten/lengthen the statutory 3-day/15-day notice-and-cure periods, since both are waivable and frequently negotiated.
Anticipate the rent-deposit/court-registry requirement in contested nonpayment cases when drafting rent-payment and default-dispute provisions.
sourceNotes: Statutory authorities reviewed: Fla. Stat. §§ 83.05, 83.06, 83.20(2), (3), 83.21, 83.22, 83.231, 83.251 (Chapter 83, Part I — Nonresidential Tenancies). Current statutory text and section numbering were confirmed against the 2025 Florida Statutes; no material change to the substance of the commercial notice, self-help, jurisdiction, timing, or damages provisions was identified for 2023–2026, notwithstanding routine non-substantive chapter-law citations appearing in the statutes' amendment history.

sections.heading: Statutory Notice
sections.text: Georgia imposes no default statutory pre-suit notice requirement for a commercial dispossessory action; notice obligations exist only to the extent the lease itself requires them. A dispossessory affidavit/demand for possession under O.C.G.A. § 44-7-50 effectively doubles as the landlord's demand and the trigger for the summary proceeding — the landlord may demand possession and, if the tenant refuses to vacate or pay, immediately file. Where the lease is silent, no separate advance notice to vacate or to cure is statutorily mandated before filing.

sections.heading: Self-Help / Commercial Lockout
sections.text: Georgia law does not categorically prohibit self-help for commercial tenancies, but it is not available as a default remedy either — a landlord may lawfully change locks or otherwise exclude a defaulting commercial tenant only where the lease expressly authorizes self-help and the exclusion can be accomplished without a breach of the peace. Georgia courts have not clearly defined "breach of the peace" in this context, which creates real exposure even where the lease authorizes the remedy, and most commercial landlords and their counsel favor the judicial dispossessory process specifically because a completed dispossessory judgment forecloses later wrongful-eviction and trespass claims.

sections.heading: Jurisdiction and Venue
sections.text: The landlord may combine a claim for possession with a claim for rent and other damages in the same dispossessory proceeding, filed in the magistrate, state, or civil court (as applicable) of the county where the property is located. O.C.G.A. §§ 44-7-49, 44-7-55(a).

sections.heading: Timing
sections.text: After the dispossessory affidavit is filed and served, the tenant has seven days to answer (orally or in writing), with the deadline extended to the next non-weekend/non-holiday day if the seventh day falls on a Saturday, Sunday, or legal holiday. O.C.G.A. § 44-7-51. If the tenant fails to answer, the court will issue a writ of possession without a hearing; if the tenant answers, the matter proceeds to trial. Georgia law also affords a tenant a statutory defense — full payment of rent owed plus dispossessory costs within the seven-day answer period bars the eviction once in any twelve-month period — but the lease may expressly override this defense, and commercial leases commonly do. O.C.G.A. § 44-7-52. Once judgment issues, the writ of possession becomes executable after seven days, and the landlord must apply for execution within thirty days, directing the sheriff to remove the tenant and its property. O.C.G.A. §§ 44-7-53, 44-7-55.

sections.heading: Damages
sections.text: Rent acceleration clauses are enforceable in Georgia commercial leases if expressly provided for, though a successful dispossessory judgment ordinarily terminates the lease and the tenant's obligation for future rent unless the lease preserves that obligation. Georgia imposes no general statutory duty on a commercial landlord to mitigate damages following a tenant default.

sections.heading: Special Considerations
sections.text: Georgia enacted the "Safe at Home Act" (H.B. 404) in 2024, adding a pre-filing cure notice and other tenant protections to O.C.G.A. Chapter 44-7 — but those provisions apply only to residential lease agreements entered into or renewed on or after July 1, 2024, and do not extend the cure-notice requirement to commercial tenancies. Commercial landlords and counsel should not assume the residential cure-notice reform changes the commercial dispossessory timeline described above.

leaseConsiderations: Express, unambiguous self-help/re-entry provision if the parties intend to preserve that remedy, paired with a "no breach of the peace" limitation acknowledgment.
Express waiver of the twelve-month statutory cure defense under O.C.G.A. § 44-7-52.
Express contractual notice-and-cure periods, since none apply by default.
Rent acceleration clause stated expressly, with survival-of-damages language after repossession.
Express disclaimer of any duty to mitigate, to avoid ambiguity given the absence of a statutory mitigation duty.
Attorney's fees provision (Georgia does not bar commercial fee-shifting clauses the way it restricts them in residential URLTA-style statutes elsewhere).
Reservation of the right to seek both possession and damages in the same dispossessory action.
sourceNotes:
Statutory authorities reviewed: O.C.G.A. §§ 44-7-49, 44-7-50, 44-7-51, 44-7-52, 44-7-53, 44-7-55(a) (dispossessory proceedings, Article 3); O.C.G.A. § 44-7-14 (tort liability of landlord, reviewed and found inapplicable to self-help authority); H.B. 404 ("Safe at Home Act"), effective July 1, 2024, reviewed and confirmed residential-only in application; 2024 Ga. Laws 484, amending O.C.G.A. § 44-7-55, reviewed and confirmed as addressing writ-of-possession/personal-property mechanics rather than the commercial notice or timing framework described above.

sections.heading: Statutory Notice
sections.text: A landlord seeking to recover possession following termination or forfeiture of a commercial lease must give the tenant a written notice to quit of at least ten days before restoring possession. Haw. Rev. Stat. § 666-1. No 2023–2026 amendment to this notice period was identified.

sections.heading: Self-Help / Commercial Lockout
sections.text: Self-help is not available by default, but Hawaii permits a landlord to exercise self-help to regain possession where the lease expressly grants that right. Outside an express lease grant, a landlord must use the summary possession process, and a wrongful, non-court-ordered exclusion overnight can expose the landlord to a statutory penalty of two months' rent (or two months' free occupancy) plus costs and attorney's fees.

sections.heading: Jurisdiction and Venue
sections.text: An action for summary possession must be brought in the district court of the circuit where the premises are located, and a landlord may join claims for rent and damages with the possession claim. Haw. Rev. Stat. §§ 666-6, 666-7.

sections.heading: Timing
sections.text: A commercial summary possession proceeding can resolve in as little as five to ten days after service if uncontested, but can extend to four to six weeks or longer where a trial is required.

sections.heading: Damages
sections.text: A rent acceleration clause is enforceable only if expressly stated in the lease. Hawaii imposes a duty on the landlord to mitigate damages, but the burden of proving a failure to mitigate rests on the tenant. Marco Kona Warehouse v. Sharmilo, Inc., 7 Haw. App. 383, 768 P.2d 247 (1989). Rent a tenant continues to pay during the pendency of a successful eviction proceeding is treated as damages for wrongful withholding of the premises rather than as ordinary rent. Haw. Rev. Stat. § 666-5.

sections.heading: Special Considerations
sections.text: Where a commercial tenant creates a statutory "nuisance," the landlord may serve a written twenty-four-hour notice to abate; if the tenant fails to comply, the landlord may then terminate the tenancy on five days' written notice following that second notice. Haw. Rev. Stat. § 666-3.

leaseConsiderations: Express self-help/re-entry authorization if the parties intend that remedy to be available.
Express rent acceleration clause, since none is implied.
Clear mitigation and reletting language, given the tenant-favorable burden-of-proof rule on mitigation.
Provisions addressing treatment of rent accepted during a pending eviction action.
Nuisance-cure procedures mirrored or modified from the twenty-four-hour/five-day statutory sequence if the parties want a different process.
Attorney's fees and cost-shifting provisions, since these are not supplied by statute for commercial leases.
sourceNotes:
Statutory authorities reviewed: Haw. Rev. Stat. §§ 666-1, 666-3, 666-5, 666-6, 666-7 (Title 36, Chapter 666, Landlord and Tenant / Summary Possession); Marco Kona Warehouse v. Sharmilo, Inc., 7 Haw. App. 383, 768 P.2d 247 (1989). No material 2023–2026 amendment to Chapter 666's commercial summary-possession provisions was located; 2026 legislative activity affecting Chapter 666 (e.g., H.B. 463's eviction-record disassociation provisions) is expressly limited to residential tenants and is not addressed here.

sections.heading: Statutory Notice
sections.text: After a commercial tenant defaults, the landlord must give three days' written notice before proceeding with an unlawful detainer action. For nonpayment, the notice must state the amount due and demand payment or possession; for breach of other lease conditions, it must demand performance or possession. The notice must also inform a commercial tenant that, if the court enters judgment for the landlord, the tenant has seven days (or longer if the court grants an extension) to remove its belongings before the landlord may remove and dispose of them — longer than the seventy-two hours given to residential tenants. Idaho Code § 6-303.

sections.heading: Self-Help / Commercial Lockout
sections.text: ⚠ Sources diverge on this point. The 2022 baseline characterized Idaho as having no statute expressly forbidding self-help. Current secondary authority, including the Idaho Legal Services Authority and practitioner commentary, describes self-help eviction — changing locks, shutting off utilities, or removing a tenant's property outside the unlawful detainer process — as unlawful in Idaho for landlords generally, and Idaho's forcible entry statute independently penalizes retaking possession by force after a tenant is in possession. Commercial landlords should not rely on lease language purporting to authorize self-help without confirming current guidance with Idaho counsel, and should expect that only the judicial unlawful detainer process reliably avoids liability.

sections.heading: Jurisdiction and Venue
sections.text: The landlord may combine an action for possession with a claim for damages, and the district court of the county where the property is located has jurisdiction. Idaho Code §§ 6-305, 6-311E.

sections.heading: Timing
sections.text: After the complaint is filed, the court must schedule trial within twelve days of filing; the summons, complaint, and notice of trial setting must be served on the defendant at least five days before trial. Idaho Code § 6-310. Following judgment, the commercial tenant has seven days (or a court-extended period) to remove belongings.

sections.heading: Damages
sections.text: Idaho's treatment of accelerated-rent clauses remains unsettled: such clauses may be collected but are not treated as enforceable liquidated-damages provisions as such, and Idaho courts examine whether the future damages sought are disproportionate to actual damages. The landlord has a duty to mitigate damages.

leaseConsiderations: Do not rely on a lease self-help clause without current Idaho counsel confirmation given the unsettled/adverse secondary authority on self-help legality.
Draft accelerated-rent provisions as a genuine pre-estimate of loss, anticipating a disproportionality challenge.
Express mitigation/reletting procedures, since a duty to mitigate applies.
Contractual notice periods longer than the three-day statutory minimum if the parties prefer more cure time.
Personal-property removal and storage procedures consistent with the seven-day statutory removal window.
Attorney's fees and cost provisions, since none are supplied by statute.
sourceNotes:
Statutory authorities reviewed: Idaho Code §§ 6-303, 6-305, 6-310, 6-311E (Title 6, Chapter 3, Forcible Entry and Unlawful Detainer). No 2023–2026 legislative amendment to these commercial provisions was identified in this research.

sections.heading: Statutory Notice
sections.text: Before filing, an Illinois landlord must make a formal demand for payment of past-due rent (or cure of the default at issue) under the state's Eviction Article (formerly styled "Forcible Entry and Detainer," renamed by P.A. 100-173). 735 Ill. Comp. Stat. 5/9-209. The landlord must give at least five days' written notice before acting on nonpayment of rent, and at least ten days' notice for all other grounds. The nonpayment notice must include statutorily prescribed language that only full payment of the amount demanded waives the landlord's termination right, unless the landlord agrees in writing to accept partial payment and continue the lease. 735 Ill. Comp. Stat. 5/9-209.

sections.heading: Self-Help / Commercial Lockout
sections.text: Self-help is not available in Illinois; the Eviction Article, 735 Ill. Comp. Stat. 5/9-101 et seq., provides the exclusive judicial procedure for regaining possession, and it applies to commercial as well as residential tenancies.

sections.heading: Jurisdiction and Venue
sections.text: The eviction action must be filed in the circuit court of the county where the property is located, and the landlord may join a claim for rent with the claim for possession. 735 Ill. Comp. Stat. 5/9-209.

sections.heading: Timing
sections.text: Timing varies materially by circuit/county docket; resolution typically takes roughly three to four months.

sections.heading: Damages
sections.text: Illinois imposes a statutory duty on the landlord to take reasonable measures to mitigate damages recoverable against a defaulting tenant. 735 Ill. Comp. Stat. 5/9-213.1.

sections.heading: Special Considerations
sections.text: A landlord should be cautious about accepting partial rent payment, since doing so (outside the statutory safe harbor described above) can be construed as an unintentional waiver of the default and may preclude eviction on that notice. Similarly, accepting keys back from a tenant before a court has entered an eviction order can be construed as a voluntary surrender of the lease and may jeopardize the landlord's ability to collect future rent.

leaseConsiderations: Express non-waiver language addressing partial-payment acceptance, tracking but reinforcing the statutory safe harbor.
Express procedures preventing return of keys/possession from being construed as surrender before judgment.
Mitigation and reletting provisions consistent with the statutory duty to mitigate.
Realistic timeline expectations (three to four months) built into any default remedies or guaranty triggers.
Attorney's fees and cost-shifting provisions.
Acceleration-of-rent language, since Illinois eviction law does not supply one by default.
sourceNotes:
Statutory authorities reviewed: 735 Ill. Comp. Stat. 5/9-209, 5/9-211, 5/9-213.1 (Code of Civil Procedure, Article IX, "Eviction," renamed from "Forcible Entry and Detainer" by P.A. 100-173, effective January 1, 2018). No material 2023–2026 amendment specific to the commercial notice, self-help, or mitigation provisions discussed above was identified; a 2025 amendment barring minors from being named as eviction defendants was reviewed and is not commercially significant.

sections.heading: Statutory Notice
sections.text: The parties may contractually waive statutory notice. Absent a waiver, a landlord terminating a tenancy and bringing an action for ejectment must give the tenant no less than ten days' notice. Ind. Code § 32-31-1-6. Notice is not required in several defined circumstances, including a fixed-term tenancy that has run its course, a tenancy at will where waste is committed, a tenancy at sufferance, or a lease requiring advance rent payment that the tenant fails to make. Ind. Code § 32-31-1-8.

sections.heading: Self-Help / Commercial Lockout
sections.text: Indiana does not recognize a general or absolute right of landlord self-help; the more consistently supported basis for self-help is where the tenant has abandoned the premises, and commercial parties sometimes attempt to reserve a contractual self-help right, but Indiana courts and regulators generally treat non-judicial lockouts, utility shutoffs, and similar exclusionary conduct as improper outside abandonment, exposing a landlord who acts unilaterally to liability.

sections.heading: Jurisdiction and Venue
sections.text: Indiana commercial possession actions are generally brought as ejectment/possession actions under Ind. Code art. 32-30, and in most counties proceed as a two-step process: an initial hearing (typically set two to three weeks after filing) determines only who is entitled to possession, with a separate, later hearing (often roughly two months out) to determine damages owed. After judgment, the landlord may pursue proceedings supplemental to collect.

sections.heading: Timing
sections.text: Possession is generally determined in under a month; damages determinations often take three to four months, varying by county docket.

sections.heading: Damages
sections.text: A rent acceleration clause is enforceable if expressly stated in the lease. As a general matter, eviction terminates the lease and future rent liability unless the lease preserves it. Where a tenant abandons the premises, the landlord has a duty to make reasonable efforts to relet and mitigate damages.

leaseConsiderations: Express notice-waiver language if the parties intend to bypass the ten-day statutory notice.
Express, narrowly tailored self-help provision limited to abandonment scenarios, given the uncertainty around self-help outside that context.
Express acceleration-of-rent and survival-of-damages provisions.
Contractual timeline/damages-hearing coordination language, given the bifurcated possession/damages process.
Mitigation and reletting cooperation provisions.
Proceedings-supplemental/judgment-collection considerations built into guaranty or security provisions.
sourceNotes:
Statutory authorities reviewed: Ind. Code §§ 32-31-1-6, 32-31-1-8 (notice); Ind. Code art. 32-30, ch. 3 (ejectment and recovery of possession of real estate). No 2023–2026 legislative amendment materially affecting these commercial provisions was identified.

sections.heading: Statutory Notice
sections.text: Before a forcible entry and detainer action may be brought, the landlord must give the tenant three days' written notice to quit. Iowa Code § 648.3.

sections.heading: Self-Help / Commercial Lockout
sections.text: ⚠ No Iowa statute expressly authorizes or forbids commercial self-help, but current secondary guidance (including Iowa Legal Aid) treats non-judicial lockouts, utility shutoffs, or exclusion of a tenant without notice and a court process as improper, and describes such self-help as exposing a landlord to suit for damages and repossession. Commercial landlords should not assume a lease self-help clause is safely enforceable without confirming current treatment with Iowa counsel.

sections.heading: Jurisdiction and Venue
sections.text: A forcible entry and detainer action must be brought in the county where the property is located. Iowa Code § 648.5. Forcible entry and detainer claims may not be joined with other claims except a claim for rent, and where a damages claim is joined it proceeds under a separate case number and timeline from the possession claim. Iowa Code § 648.19.

sections.heading: Timing
sections.text: Once the petition is filed, the court must set the hearing no later than eight days after filing, or no later than fifteen days after filing with the plaintiff's consent. Iowa Code § 648.5.

sections.heading: Damages
sections.text: There is no expedited statutory remedy to recover delinquent rent apart from the possession action. A rent acceleration clause is enforceable only if expressly stated in the lease. The landlord's duty to mitigate applies only where the tenant has abandoned the premises.

leaseConsiderations: Do not rely on an unqualified self-help clause without confirming current Iowa treatment; consider limiting any self-help right to post-abandonment scenarios.
Express acceleration-of-rent clause, since none is implied.
Coordinate any damages claim strategy with the separate case-number/timeline requirement for joined rent claims.
Express mitigation obligations if the parties want mitigation to apply beyond the abandonment context.
Contractual notice periods longer than three days if additional cure time is desired.
Attorney's fees provisions, since none are supplied by statute.
sourceNotes:
Statutory authorities reviewed: Iowa Code §§ 648.3, 648.5, 648.19 (Forcible Entry and Detainer, Title XV, Chapter 648). No 2023–2026 amendment materially affecting these commercial provisions was identified; a 2024 amendment to Iowa Code § 648.22 (H.F. 548, effective July 1, 2024) addressing court-record aggregation and reporting for forcible entry and detainer actions was reviewed and found to be procedural/record-keeping in nature rather than substantively affecting commercial notice, self-help, jurisdiction, timing, or damages.

sections.heading: Statutory Notice
sections.text: A Kansas landlord must give the tenant three days' notice to leave the premises for which possession is sought before filing an eviction lawsuit. Kan. Stat. Ann. § 61-3803. The three-day period is computed as three consecutive 24-hour periods beginning when the notice is delivered, posted, or mailed; if mailed, an additional two days is added; and Saturdays, Sundays, legal holidays, and days the clerk's office is closed do not count toward the period. Id.

sections.heading: Self-Help / Commercial Lockout
sections.text: There is no right to use self-help in Kansas. Kan. Stat. Ann. § 61-3804.

sections.heading: Jurisdiction and Venue
sections.text: A landlord may bring an action for rent due together with the possession action, or may pursue a separate rent action for the amount due. A judgment in the eviction action does not bar a subsequent lawsuit by either party for claims not included in that judgment. Kan. Stat. Ann. §§ 61-3802, 61-3804.

sections.heading: Timing
sections.text: The defendant must appear on the date in the summons, which must be no less than three and no more than fourteen days after the summons issues. If trial is necessary, it must occur within fourteen days after the appearance date in the summons. Kan. Stat. Ann. §§ 61-3805, 61-3806, 61-3807.

sections.heading: Damages
sections.text: Acceleration-of-rent clauses are likely enforceable in Kansas, though some case law cuts against enforceability. A landlord may seek rent due together with the possession claim. Kan. Stat. Ann. § 61-3804.

leaseConsiderations: Express rent acceleration clause, given the mixed case law on enforceability absent express lease language.
No reliance on self-help; build default remedies around the judicial eviction timeline.
Careful computation of the three-day notice period (24-hour blocks, mail add-on, and excluded days) built into any contractual notice mechanics.
Consider whether to pursue rent and possession jointly or reserve the rent claim separately, given the non-bar rule for unincluded claims.
Attorney's fees provisions, since none are supplied by statute.
Contractual notice periods longer than three days if desired.
sourceNotes:
Statutory authorities reviewed: Kan. Stat. Ann. §§ 61-3802, 61-3803, 61-3804, 61-3805, 61-3806, 61-3807 (Chapter 61, Article 38, Evictions). No 2023–2026 amendment materially affecting these commercial provisions was identified.

sections.heading: Statutory Notice
sections.text: ⚠ Correction to the 2022 baseline: the fixed seven-day (nonpayment) and fourteen-day (other breach) notice periods found in KRS § 383.660 are part of Kentucky's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, KRS §§ 383.500–383.715, which by its terms governs only residential dwelling units and applies only in the specific counties and cities that have formally adopted it (e.g., Louisville-Jefferson County, Lexington-Fayette County, and a handful of others) — it does not govern commercial tenancies anywhere in the Commonwealth. For a commercial tenancy, notice to terminate for default or holdover is governed by the lease and Kentucky common law rather than a fixed statutory period; the forcible detainer action itself, applicable to commercial and residential tenancies alike, is defined and governed by KRS § 383.200 et seq.

sections.heading: Self-Help / Commercial Lockout
sections.text: ⚠ Correction to the 2022 baseline: the self-help prohibition of KRS § 383.655 is also a URLTA (residential-only) provision and does not, by its terms, bar self-help in a commercial tenancy. Secondary authority identifies Kentucky as among the states with no statute or reported decision squarely prohibiting commercial self-help, meaning a common-law self-help remedy may remain available where the lease reserves it — but Kentucky courts, like courts generally, tend to disfavor a landlord's use of self-help because it forces a tenant out before the tenant can litigate its right to remain in possession, so counsel should weigh this risk carefully even where no statute forecloses the remedy.

sections.heading: Jurisdiction and Venue
sections.text: Forcible detainer actions are heard in Kentucky district court, with appeal to circuit court. KRS § 383.200 et seq.

sections.heading: Timing
sections.text: After judgment, the tenant is ordered to vacate within seven days, and either party may appeal to circuit court within seven days of the judgment's entry. KRS §§ 383.240, 383.255.

sections.heading: Damages
sections.text: ⚠ Because the treble-holdover-damages remedy (KRS § 383.695), the attorney's-fee-clause prohibition (KRS § 383.570), and the related damages provisions cited in the 2022 baseline are also URLTA (residential-only) provisions, they do not apply to a commercial tenancy. Commercial rent acceleration, mitigation, and attorney's-fee-shifting are instead governed by the lease and Kentucky common contract-law principles; this research could not independently verify Kentucky-specific case law resolving the enforceability of a commercial acceleration clause against a penalty/liquidated-damages challenge or confirming the scope of any mitigation duty. Confirm current commercial-damages case law with Kentucky counsel before relying on a specific acceleration or mitigation position.

sections.heading: Special Considerations
sections.text: Because the residential URLTA framework does not apply to commercial tenancies, a commercial lease is the primary — and often only — source of the parties' notice, cure, self-help, and damages rights in Kentucky; unlike many other states, there is little statutory backstop protecting a commercial tenant absent express lease terms.

leaseConsiderations: Express notice-and-cure provisions, since no fixed statutory notice period applies to commercial leases.
Express, carefully limited self-help/re-entry clause if the parties want to preserve that remedy, paired with breach-of-the-peace and risk-allocation language.
Express rent acceleration clause with a genuine pre-estimate-of-loss rationale, anticipating a possible penalty challenge.
Express duty-to-mitigate (or disclaimer of mitigation) language, since the statutory mitigation duty does not extend to commercial tenancies.
Express attorney's-fee-shifting clause, since the URLTA fee-clause prohibition does not apply to commercial leases.
Contractual timeline coordination given the compressed seven-day post-judgment vacate and seven-day appeal windows.
sourceNotes:
Statutory authorities reviewed: KRS §§ 383.200, 383.210, 383.240, 383.255 (Chapter 383, forcible entry and detainer, applicable to all tenancies); KRS §§ 383.500, 383.570, 383.655, 383.660, 383.695, 383.705 (Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, confirmed via multiple secondary sources — including Kentucky Legal Services Authority and University of Kentucky College of Law commentary — to apply only to residential dwelling units in adopting localities). ⚠ Commercial-specific case law on acceleration-clause enforceability and mitigation could not be independently verified in this research; confirm with local counsel.

sections.heading: Statutory Notice
sections.text: When a lessee's right of occupancy has ceased — whether by expiration of the lease term, action of the lessor, nonpayment of rent, or otherwise — and the lessor wishes to obtain possession, the lessor must deliver written notice to vacate, giving the lessee not less than five days from delivery to vacate. La. Code Civ. Proc. art. 4701. A lessee may waive this notice by written waiver in the lease, in which case the lessor may institute eviction proceedings immediately upon termination of the right of occupancy. Id.

sections.heading: Self-Help / Commercial Lockout
sections.text: No self-help remedy is available in Louisiana. Commercial landlords must repossess leased premises only through a court order authorizing eviction, executed by a government official such as a representative of the local sheriff's office; the landlord may not carry out the dispossession itself.

sections.heading: Jurisdiction and Venue
sections.text: The landlord must file separate actions for possession and for damages. The possession action must be filed in the parish court, city court, or justice of the peace court (as applicable) where the property is located. Effective August 1, 2024, La. Code Civ. Proc. art. 4844, as amended by Acts 2024, No. 129, gives parish and city courts jurisdiction concurrent with the district courts over eviction suits — including suits to evict occupants or tenants of leased commercial premises — without regard to the dollar amount of rent or the value of the right of occupancy involved, removing the jurisdictional dollar thresholds that previously constrained parish/city court jurisdiction in higher-rent commercial matters.

sections.heading: Timing
sections.text: An eviction proceeding is typically completed within thirty to sixty days. The eviction hearing may not be held earlier than three days after service of the eviction suit, though the actual date depends on the court's docket.

sections.heading: Damages
sections.text: A rent acceleration clause must be expressly provided for in the lease to be enforceable. A landlord may not continue collecting rent after the lease has been terminated.

sections.heading: Special Considerations
sections.text: There is no right to a jury trial on eviction matters in Louisiana.

sections.heading: 2026 Update Note
sections.text: Effective August 1, 2024, Acts 2024, No. 129 amended and re-enacted La. Code Civ. Proc. art. 4844 to give parish and city courts jurisdiction concurrent with district courts over eviction proceedings — including commercial-lease and farmland evictions — regardless of the daily, monthly, or yearly rental amount or the annual value of the right of occupancy, eliminating the prior dollar-based jurisdictional caps for those courts in commercial matters.

leaseConsiderations: Express written waiver of the five-day notice-to-vacate requirement if immediate suit upon default is desired.
Express rent acceleration clause, since none is implied by law.
Post-termination rent-collection limitations built into any holdover or damages provisions, given the bar on continuing to collect rent after termination.
Venue selection clause anticipating concurrent parish/city and district court jurisdiction post-2024 amendment.
Provisions addressing the mandatory separate-action structure for possession versus damages claims.
Jury-trial-waiver acknowledgment, consistent with the statutory bar on jury trials in eviction matters.
sourceNotes: Statutory authorities reviewed: La. Code Civ. Proc. arts. 4701, 4702, 4732 (notice to vacate, timing), and 4844 (jurisdiction); Acts 2024, No. 129, amending La. Code Civ. Proc. art. 4844, effective August 1, 2024.

sections.heading: Statutory Notice
sections.text: Maine's Forcible Entry and Detainer statute, 14 M.R.S. §§ 6001–6046, is divided into Subchapter 1 (Residential Landlords and Tenants, §§ 6000–6016-A) and Subchapter 2 (Commercial Leases, § 6017 et seq.). The seven-day pay-or-quit notice found at 14 M.R.S. § 6002 applies only to residential tenancies under Subchapter 1 — it does not govern commercial leases. Commercial tenancies are instead governed by 14 M.R.S. § 6017, which does not itself impose a statutory pre-filing notice period; notice requirements for a commercial default are therefore set by the lease and ordinary contract principles, not by a fixed statutory number of days. Practitioners relying on a "seven-day notice" for a Maine commercial matter are relying on the wrong subchapter.

sections.heading: Self-Help / Commercial Lockout
sections.text: The self-help prohibition at 14 M.R.S. § 6014 likewise sits in Subchapter 1 and by its terms governs residential tenancies. No parallel statutory self-help ban applies expressly to commercial leases under Subchapter 2, and no Maine appellate authority was located squarely addressing self-help repossession of commercial premises. ⚠ Could not independently verify the availability of self-help for Maine commercial landlords with confidence — commercial landlords should not assume self-help is available absent express lease authorization and should confirm current guidance with local counsel before attempting extrajudicial repossession.

sections.heading: Jurisdiction and Venue
sections.text: The District Court has jurisdiction to hear, decide, and award rent and arrears allegedly owing in a commercial tenancy dispute, regardless of the amount in controversy. 14 M.R.S. § 6017.

sections.heading: Timing
sections.text: Timing is variable and depends on the District Court's docket. Under § 6017, a tenant defending a commercial forcible entry and detainer action must appear on the return date and pay the agreed-upon rent, including all arrears, as a condition of maintaining the defense; disputed amounts are determined by the court at hearing. If the tenant fails to pay rent to the court when due, the writ of possession issues immediately. Where judgment favors the landlord, the court may issue the writ of possession immediately — including during a Superior Court appeal — if the landlord posts a surety bond conditioned on paying damages and costs the tenant may suffer if the tenant ultimately prevails.

sections.heading: Damages
sections.text: Maine's statutory landlord's-duty-to-mitigate provision, 14 M.R.S. § 6010-A, is likewise confined to Subchapter 1 residential tenancies. No parallel statutory mitigation duty applies to Maine commercial leases, consistent with the 2022 baseline's conclusion that a commercial landlord has no duty to mitigate damages, though the lease itself may impose one.

sections.heading: Special Considerations
sections.text: A commercial landlord and tenant may agree, in the lease or in a separate agreement, to waive a jury trial for disputes arising from the lease, and may likewise agree to binding arbitration, with an arbitrator's decision favoring the landlord permitting immediate writ issuance upon docketing with the Superior Court under the Uniform Arbitration Act. 14 M.R.S. § 6017. Lease language should be reviewed carefully to avoid inadvertently sweeping a possession dispute into a mandatory arbitration clause. As noted above, a tenant must pay rent in arrears to maintain a defense once an action is filed.

leaseConsiderations: Define the notice period and cure rights expressly, since no statutory commercial notice period exists to fall back on.
Include an express, clearly drafted jury trial waiver if a bench proceeding is preferred.
Consider an arbitration clause but carve out possession disputes to avoid delaying repossession.
Include an explicit self-help/re-entry clause only after consulting Maine counsel, given the absence of clear statutory or case authority on commercial self-help.
Address mitigation obligations directly in the lease, since no statutory duty to mitigate applies to commercial tenancies.
Provide for acceleration of rent and attorney's fees expressly, as neither is guaranteed by statute.
Specify electronic and alternative notice-delivery methods in the lease.

sections.heading: Statutory Notice
sections.text: Maryland does not require a landlord to give a commercial tenant statutory pre-filing notice before bringing a Failure to Pay Rent action; the 10-day written notice-of-intent-to-file requirement added to Md. Code Ann., Real Prop. § 8-401 is expressly limited to residential premises. For a commercial tenant holding over or breaching a lease, however, Real Property § 8-402 (holding over) and § 8-402.1 (breach of lease) apply to both residential and commercial tenancies and require 30 days' written notice of the breach and the landlord's intent to repossess (14 days where the tenant's conduct poses a clear and imminent danger of serious harm to persons or property). Commercial landlords should therefore not assume no notice is ever required — the answer depends on which of Maryland's several summary ejectment causes of action is being pursued.

sections.heading: Self-Help / Commercial Lockout
sections.text: Self-help remedies remain available to a commercial landlord in Maryland, provided they are exercised peaceably and without breaching the peace. K & K Mgmt., Inc. v. Lee, 316 Md. 137, 557 A.2d 965, 979–80 (1989). The remedy generally requires that the tenant be in default beyond any applicable cure period, that the lease authorize re-entry, and that repossession occur without violence, threats, or confrontation. Maryland's courts have reaffirmed the remedy but continue to discourage its use given the practical risks of a breach-of-the-peace dispute. Donegal Assocs., LLC v. Christie-Scott, LLC, 248 Md. App. 631 (2020).

sections.heading: Jurisdiction and Venue
sections.text: A landlord may seek possession and monetary damages in the same District Court proceeding. If damages sought exceed the constitutional jury-trial threshold, a party may demand a jury trial and have the case removed from the District Court to the Circuit Court. Md. Code Ann., Cts. & Jud. Proc. § 4-402(e). That threshold was raised from $15,000 to $25,000 by constitutional amendment approved by Maryland voters in November 2022, effective December 4, 2022 — meaning the $15,000 figure in the 2022 baseline is now outdated and should be treated as $25,000 going forward.

sections.heading: Timing
sections.text: For a Failure to Pay Rent case, the court issues a summons for trial on the fifth day after the complaint is filed. Md. Code Ann., Real Prop. § 8-401. Removal to Circuit Court on a jury demand can add several months before trial.

sections.heading: Damages
sections.text: A Maryland commercial landlord has a duty to mitigate damages, and rent-acceleration clauses are enforceable if expressly stated in the lease.

sections.heading: Special Considerations
sections.text: Where a damages case is removed to Circuit Court, the tenant is generally required to continue paying rent pending trial. Where the landlord is awarded a judgment of restitution, the tenant retains a statutory right of redemption by tendering all past-due amounts, court costs, and fees before actual execution of the eviction order. Real Prop. § 8-401(e).

sections.heading: 2026 Update Note
sections.text: Effective October 1, 2024, the Renters' Rights and Stabilization Act of 2024 (2024 Md. Laws, H.B. 693) increased the waiting period between a judgment of possession and execution of the warrant of restitution from four to seven days, applicable to both residential and commercial ejectment cases, and substantially increased the District and Circuit Court surcharges assessed in summary ejectment and non-summary ejectment cases.

leaseConsiderations: Expressly authorize re-entry/self-help in the lease if the landlord wants to preserve that remedy, with clear default and cure triggers.
Draft default notice provisions tracking whichever of §§ 8-401, 8-402, or 8-402.1 will actually apply to the anticipated breach.
Include an express mitigation and reletting clause.
Include an enforceable, clearly stated acceleration clause.
Build in extra time for possible removal to Circuit Court on a jury demand above $25,000.
Address attorney's fees and cost-shifting expressly.
Consider a redemption-rights waiver where permitted, given the statutory tenant redemption right.
sourceNotes:
Statutory authorities reviewed: Md. Code Ann., Real Prop. §§ 8-401, 8-402, 8-402.1; Md. Code Ann., Cts. & Jud. Proc. § 4-402(e); K & K Mgmt., Inc. v. Lee, 316 Md. 137 (1989); Donegal Assocs., LLC v. Christie-Scott, LLC, 248 Md. App. 631 (2020); Renters' Rights and Stabilization Act of 2024, H.B. 693 (2024 Md. Laws), effective October 1, 2024; Maryland constitutional amendment raising the jury-trial threshold to $25,000, effective December 4, 2022.

sections.heading: Statutory Notice
sections.text: When a commercial tenant defaults on rent, the landlord may terminate under the notice provisions specified in the lease. In the absence of such lease provisions, the landlord must give the tenant at least 14 days' written notice. Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 11A.

sections.heading: Self-Help / Commercial Lockout
sections.text: Self-help remedies are not available in Massachusetts, even for commercial tenants. Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 184, § 18 prohibits forcible or self-help entry to recover possession of land or tenements and requires that possession be recovered through judicial process; unlawful lockouts and utility shutoffs can also carry criminal penalties.

sections.heading: Jurisdiction and Venue
sections.text: Recovering possession (summary process) and recovering damages may require separate lawsuits. In a summary process case the landlord may sue for unpaid rent even where the tenancy was terminated for a reason other than nonpayment, but the landlord cannot include claims for other damages, such as property damage, in the summary process action — those require a separate civil suit.

sections.heading: Timing
sections.text: Summary process to regain possession typically takes roughly 17 to 40 days after filing. The timing of a separate suit for non-rent damages depends on the court's docket and is variable. The Trial Court solicited public comment through November 2025 on proposed amendments to the Uniform Summary Process Rules addressing filing and service mechanics; as of this writing those amendments had not been finalized, so no substantive rule change is reported here.

sections.heading: Damages
sections.text: If the landlord does not terminate the lease, the landlord has no duty to mitigate damages. A rent-acceleration clause is enforceable if expressly provided for in the lease and does not constitute a penalty.

leaseConsiderations: Include an express notice-and-cure provision to avoid defaulting to the 14-day statutory notice.
Draft a rent-acceleration clause carefully to avoid characterization as an unenforceable penalty.
Reserve the landlord's right to pursue non-rent damages in a separate civil action.
Include express mitigation language if the parties intend a different mitigation standard than the no-duty default (applicable only where the lease is not terminated).
Include an attorney's fees provision.
Confirm self-help is not authorized by the lease, since it is unavailable under Massachusetts law regardless of lease language.
sourceNotes:
Statutory authorities reviewed: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 11A; Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 184, § 18; Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 239 (Summary Process for Possession of Land).
