sections.heading: Statutory Notice
sections.text: Seven days' notice is required after the landlord serves a written demand for possession for nonpayment of rent; after the seven-day period, the landlord may recover possession by summary proceedings. Mich. Comp. Laws § 600.5714.

sections.heading: Self-Help / Commercial Lockout
sections.text: Self-help is prohibited under Michigan law. The Anti-Lockout Statute, MCL § 600.2918, makes it unlawful for a landlord to forcibly remove or exclude a tenant, or to willfully interrupt utility service, to recover possession, and its protections may not be waived. A tenant forcibly and unlawfully put out may recover three times actual damages or $200, whichever is greater, plus possession; a tenant otherwise unlawfully interfered with (e.g., by lockout or utility shutoff) may recover actual damages or $200, whichever is greater, for each occurrence.

sections.heading: Jurisdiction and Venue
sections.text: A landlord may join a claim for damages with the claim for possession of the premises; however, the court may order separate disposition of the possession and damages claims. Mich. Comp. Laws § 600.5739.

sections.heading: Timing
sections.text: The court issues a summons directing the defendant to appear for trial within 30 days of the summons's issuance date, with the summons served not less than 10 days before the trial date. Mich. Comp. Laws § 600.5735. If judgment is entered for the landlord, the court issues a writ of restitution.

sections.heading: Damages
sections.text: A landlord has a duty to mitigate damages when a tenant abandons the premises and stops paying rent due under the lease. An acceleration-of-rent clause may be enforceable, but under the Truth in Renting Act, MCL § 554.633(1)(i), (k), a lease provision purporting to release a party from the duty to mitigate is void, and an acceleration clause must allow that the tenant may not be liable for the full accelerated amount because of the landlord's mitigation obligation, with either party entitled to have a court determine the actual amount owed. Mich. Comp. Laws § 600.5726 addresses the related but distinct context of accelerated indebtedness on forfeiture of a land contract.

sections.heading: Special Considerations
sections.text: A tenant may attempt to delay the eviction hearing by filing a related action in a higher court and requesting a stay of the summary proceeding pending resolution of that action; the tenant's separate lawsuit must involve the leased premises and the eviction issue.

leaseConsiderations: Draft an acceleration clause that expressly preserves the tenant's right to a judicial determination of actual damages, consistent with MCL § 554.633.
Do not attempt to waive the statutory mitigation duty — such waivers are void.
Include a clear demand-for-possession and notice mechanism tracking the seven-day requirement.
Address whether possession and damages claims will be pursued together or reserved for separate disposition.
Include an attorney's fees provision.
Anticipate potential delay tactics via related litigation and consider forum-selection and venue clauses.
sourceNotes:
Statutory authorities reviewed: Mich. Comp. Laws §§ 600.5714, 600.5726, 600.5735, 600.5739, 600.2918; Truth in Renting Act, MCL § 554.633.

sections.heading: Statutory Notice
sections.text: Unless required by the lease, a commercial landlord in Minnesota generally need not give the tenant statutory notice before bringing an eviction action. The 14-day pre-filing notice requirement added to Minn. Stat. § 504B.321, subd. 1a is, by its express terms, limited to residential tenants and does not apply to commercial leases.

sections.heading: Self-Help / Commercial Lockout
sections.text: Minnesota does not permit a commercial landlord to use self-help to dispossess a tenant who remains in possession; possession must be recovered through a judicial eviction action. Where a commercial tenant has actually abandoned the premises, however, a landlord may take possession of and deal with the tenant's remaining personal property under Minn. Stat. § 504B.271, without that step itself constituting an unlawful eviction, since no person remains in possession to dispossess.

sections.heading: Jurisdiction and Venue
sections.text: An eviction action may combine allegations of nonpayment of rent and material violation of the lease, though they are heard as alternative grounds. Minn. Stat. § 504B.285.

sections.heading: Timing
sections.text: A hearing takes place between seven and 14 days after the summons is issued. Minn. Stat. § 504B.321. The 2023 amendments repealed the prior six-day cap on scheduling eviction trials, directing courts instead to set trial dates that allow "fair, thorough, and timely adjudication," considering case complexity, discovery needs, and preparation time — a change that applies to commercial as well as residential eviction trials, though courts must still prioritize scheduling of residential (not commercial) cases involving safety-endangerment allegations.

sections.heading: Damages
sections.text: A landlord has no duty to mitigate damages unless the landlord has accepted the tenant's abandonment of the premises. Rent-acceleration clauses are enforceable.

sections.heading: 2026 Update Note
sections.text: Effective January 1, 2024, Minnesota Laws 2023, chapter 52 (article 19), amended Minn. Stat. §§ 504B.285 and 504B.321 to, among other things, repeal the former six-day cap on eviction trial scheduling, expand the required content of eviction complaints (including an itemized accounting for nonpayment claims and identification of the specific lease provision breached), permit additional written-communication methods for landlord notices, restrict bond requirements, and require courts to dismiss and expunge actions where filing and service requirements are not met. These procedural changes apply to commercial evictions filed under Chapter 504B, though most of the Act's substantive tenant protections remain residential-only.

leaseConsiderations: Draft an express notice-and-cure clause, since no statutory notice period applies to commercial defaults.
Include an acceleration clause, as these remain generally enforceable.
Address mitigation expressly, since the statutory no-duty default applies except on accepted abandonment.
Anticipate longer, less predictable trial scheduling following the 2024 repeal of the six-day cap.
Ensure any eviction complaint will include the itemized rent accounting or specific lease-breach detail now expected under § 504B.321.
Address handling of abandoned personal property consistent with § 504B.271.
Include an attorney's fees provision.
sourceNotes:
Statutory authorities reviewed: Minn. Stat. §§ 504B.285, 504B.321, 504B.271; Minnesota Laws 2023, ch. 52, art. 19 (eff. Jan. 1, 2024, for leases entered into or renewed on or after that date).

sections.heading: Statutory Notice
sections.text: A landlord must give a defaulting commercial tenant three days' written notice to pay rent or quit the premises. Miss. Code Ann. § 89-7-27. Any default condition expressed in a written lease may also trigger the eviction process, and notice of default by email or text message is proper where the tenant has agreed in writing to that method of notice. If the tenant does not vacate within the notice period, the landlord may terminate the tenancy and file suit. Id.

sections.heading: Self-Help / Commercial Lockout
sections.text: Mississippi permits self-help under limited circumstances: the written lease must specifically authorize the landlord's re-entry upon a lease violation, the landlord must give the tenant three days' written notice, and the landlord must not break in, use violence, or threaten violence in retaking possession.

sections.heading: Jurisdiction and Venue
sections.text: A landlord may bring an action for possession of the premises together with an action for rent in the same proceeding.

sections.heading: Timing
sections.text: An eviction proceeding typically takes roughly six weeks to nine months, depending on the court's docket. A tenant has seven days from the date of judgment to move out, unless the court orders otherwise based on the circumstances. Miss. Code Ann. § 89-7-31.

sections.heading: Damages
sections.text: A rent-acceleration clause is enforceable if expressly provided for in the lease. A tenant who refuses to quit after lawful notice is liable for double rent during the holdover period. Miss. Code Ann. § 89-7-25.

sections.heading: Special Considerations
sections.text: A tenant is not required to continue paying rent for a building destroyed by fire or otherwise, unless the tenant caused the destruction or expressly agreed to keep paying rent after destruction. Miss. Code Ann. § 89-7-3.

leaseConsiderations: Include an express re-entry/self-help authorization if the landlord wants to preserve that remedy, since it is unavailable absent explicit lease language.
Authorize electronic (email/text) notice in writing to take advantage of the statutory allowance.
Include an enforceable acceleration clause.
Address holdover rent expressly, since double rent otherwise applies by statute.
Include a casualty/destruction clause addressing continued rent obligations.
Include an attorney's fees provision.
sourceNotes:
Statutory authorities reviewed: Miss. Code Ann. §§ 89-7-3, 89-7-25, 89-7-27, 89-7-31, as amended through Laws 2022, ch. 501 (S.B. 2461), effective April 21, 2022 — the most recent amendment identified to these sections as of August 2026. A bill introduced in the 2026 Regular Session (H.B. 499) proposing to shorten eviction trial-scheduling timelines was located but could not be confirmed as enacted; it is not relied upon here.

sections.heading: Statutory Notice
sections.text: No statutory notice is required in Missouri for expedited eviction proceedings under Mo. Rev. Stat. § 441.740, nor for leases that have been properly terminated under their own terms.

sections.heading: Self-Help / Commercial Lockout
sections.text: Self-help remedies are prohibited in Missouri, including for commercial tenants. Even where a lease purports to authorize self-help, a landlord who changes locks, shuts off utilities, or otherwise excludes a tenant without a court eviction risks liability for wrongful eviction and conversion, potentially including business-interruption damages exceeding the unpaid rent.

sections.heading: Jurisdiction and Venue
sections.text: Missouri provides several distinct eviction proceedings — rent-and-possession and unlawful detainer actions under Mo. Rev. Stat. ch. 535 and ch. 534, respectively, and immediate/emergency eviction under § 441.740 — filed in the circuit court for the county where the property is located. A claim for damages can generally be joined with a claim for possession, or the landlord may elect to pursue possession first and file a separate damages suit later.

sections.heading: Timing
sections.text: Timing depends entirely on the court's docket; recent rent-and-possession and unlawful detainer proceedings have taken approximately six to seven months. Expedited, "immediate eviction" proceedings remain available under § 441.740 for emergency situations.

sections.heading: Damages
sections.text: Missouri courts generally uphold damages provisions negotiated in good faith between the parties but are unlikely to enforce a penalty provision that produces a windfall for the landlord rather than compensating for actual damages; Missouri appellate courts have not squarely resolved the enforceability of rent-acceleration clauses. Missouri recognizes three options on a tenant's default: the landlord may remain out of possession and sue for rent as it becomes due; give notice of intent to re-let to mitigate damages while reserving the right to sue for unpaid rent; or re-enter, take possession, and terminate the tenant's right to possession. A landlord is entitled to double the yearly rental value for a tenant's holdover after written demand and notice to quit. Mo. Rev. Stat. § 441.080. ⚠ The 2022 baseline also asserted a double-rent remedy for unauthorized subletting or assignment (citing "§ 534.537," a section number that could not be located in the current Missouri statutes) — this could not be independently verified and should be confirmed with local counsel before relying on it; Mo. Rev. Stat. § 441.030 does bar assignment or subletting without written landlord consent for terms of two years or less, but the specific double-rent consequence for that violation could not be confirmed.

sections.heading: Special Considerations
sections.text: Missouri recognizes three general categories of eviction suits: (1) rent and possession, (2) unlawful detainer, and (3) immediate eviction, the last limited to emergencies involving risk of physical injury, substantial property damage, or drug-related criminal activity. Mo. Rev. Stat. § 441.740. Choosing between rent-and-possession and unlawful detainer largely turns on whether the landlord wants to resolve everything (possession and damages) in one proceeding or pursue possession first and damages separately.

sections.heading: 2026 Update Note
sections.text: Effective August 28, 2024, Missouri Senate Bill 895 (2024) bars counties, municipalities, and other political subdivisions from imposing or enforcing an eviction moratorium unless specifically authorized by state or federal law — foreclosing the kind of local eviction-moratorium orders some Missouri municipalities issued during the COVID-19 pandemic — and requires that transfers of title to rental property carrying an outstanding collectible judgment be filed with the circuit court within 30 days of transfer. Separately, § 441.740 was itself amended effective August 28, 2023 by Missouri Senate Bill 106 (2023); the amendment's specific substantive changes could not be independently confirmed from available secondary sources. ⚠ Confirm the precise text and effect of the 2023 amendment to § 441.740 with current Missouri statutory text or local counsel before relying on its details.

leaseConsiderations: Do not rely on lease language purporting to authorize self-help — it remains prohibited and risky regardless of lease terms.
Draft damages provisions as genuine compensation, not a penalty, given Missouri courts' skepticism of windfall clauses.
Address rent acceleration explicitly and expect potential judicial scrutiny given the unsettled case law.
Specify which eviction pathway (rent-and-possession vs. unlawful detainer vs. joined damages) the parties anticipate.
Include an express mitigation/reletting clause given the ambiguity in the common-law default rules.
Include an attorney's fees provision.
Build realistic timeline expectations into default/cure and remedy provisions given typical six-to-seven-month proceedings.
sourceNotes:
Statutory authorities reviewed: Mo. Rev. Stat. §§ 441.080, 441.740, 534.137, 535.010, 535.110; Missouri Senate Bill 895 (2024 Mo. Laws), effective August 28, 2024; Missouri Senate Bill 106 (2023 Mo. Laws), amending § 441.740 effective August 28, 2023.

sections.heading: Statutory Notice
sections.text: A landlord must provide a tenant with three days' written notice before reentry. Mont. Code Ann. § 70-27-106. Notice is not required, however, to file an action for possession of the property. Id. § 70-27-107.

sections.heading: Self-Help / Commercial Lockout
sections.text: A landlord may use self-help remedies when evicting a commercial tenant, but may not use force in retaking possession. Changing locks alone does not constitute forcible entry.

sections.heading: Jurisdiction and Venue
sections.text: A landlord may bring an action for damages together with an action for possession of the premises in the same lawsuit. Id. § 70-27-205. An action for repossession may be brought in the justice's court or the district court of the county where the property is situated. Id. § 70-27-101.

sections.heading: Timing
sections.text: In an eviction proceeding, the tenant has 10 days to answer after service of the complaint. Id. § 70-27-117. Answers filed in justice's court are tried within 10 days after the tenant's appearance or answer. Id. § 70-27-202 (recodified provisions govern trial timing under Chapter 27). If the proceeding is for nonpayment of rent, a judgment may not be enforced until five days after entry; otherwise the judgment may be enforced immediately. Id. § 70-27-205(3). Summary proceedings remain available for unlawful detainer actions. Id. § 70-16-109.

sections.heading: Damages
sections.text: A Montana landlord has a duty to mitigate damages when a tenant breaches a lease. A rent-acceleration clause must be expressly provided for in the lease to be enforced. Damages for forcible entry or unlawful detainer may be recovered at three times actual damages. Id. § 70-27-206.

sections.heading: Special Considerations
sections.text: In a nonpayment proceeding, the tenant may retain possession by paying the rent owed within five days after entry of judgment. Id. § 70-27-205(3). If a landlord accepts rent after a lease expires, the lease is presumed renewed on the same terms for the same term, not to exceed one year. Id. § 70-26-204. A 2023 bill that would have generally revised Montana landlord-tenant law (H.B. 732) died in committee and did not become law, so no material statutory change to Chapter 27 was identified for 2023–2026.

leaseConsiderations: Address self-help/re-entry procedures expressly to define the parties' expectations, even though Montana permits it by default absent force.
Include an express rent-acceleration clause, since none is implied.
Include a mitigation clause consistent with (or clarifying) the statutory duty to mitigate.
Address treble-damages exposure for any disputed forcible-entry or unlawful-detainer scenario.
Specify whether renewal is intended if rent is accepted post-expiration, to avoid an unintended one-year statutory renewal.
Include an attorney's fees provision.

sections.heading: Statutory Notice
sections.text: A landlord must give the tenant three days' written notice before proceeding with an eviction action based on a monetary default. Neb. Rev. Stat. § 25-21,221. This section applies to forcible entry and detainer actions under §§ 25-21,219 to 25-21,235, which are expressly distinct from, and do not apply to, tenancies governed by Nebraska's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act. Neb. Rev. Stat. § 25-21,219.

sections.heading: Self-Help / Commercial Lockout
sections.text: Self-help remedies are prohibited under Nebraska law.

sections.heading: Jurisdiction and Venue
sections.text: District and county courts have jurisdiction over forcible entry and detainer actions. Neb. Rev. Stat. § 25-21,219. The proceeding may determine both the right to possession of the premises and rents or other damages owed. Id.

sections.heading: Timing
sections.text: An eviction trial must take place not less than 10 days but not more than 14 days after the summons is issued. Neb. Rev. Stat. § 25-21,223. A continuance may not exceed seven days absent extraordinary cause supported by an undertaking covering accruing rent and damages. Id. § 25-21,225. The time to complete a separate action for damages is variable and depends on the court's docket.

sections.heading: Damages
sections.text: A Nebraska landlord has a duty to mitigate damages, but the tenant bears the burden of proving the landlord unreasonably failed to do so. If the landlord terminates the lease, the tenant is generally not required to pay future rent and liabilities, but a rent-acceleration clause is enforceable if expressly stated in the lease.

leaseConsiderations: Confirm the lease's default-notice provisions align with (or intentionally extend) the three-day statutory minimum.
Do not rely on self-help — it is categorically unavailable in Nebraska.
Include an express rent-acceleration clause to preserve post-termination remedies.
Address mitigation obligations and evidentiary burdens in the lease to reduce future disputes.
Include an attorney's fees provision.
Plan around the compressed 10-to-14-day trial-scheduling window when assessing litigation strategy.

Stat. §§ 25-21,219, 25-21,221, 25-21,223, 25-21,225, current as reflected on the Nebraska Legislature's official statutes site; no amendments to these specific sections were identified within the 2023–2026 window (the most recent amendment located to § 25-21,219 was Laws 2021, LB320, § 1, predating this review period).

sections.heading: Statutory Notice
sections.text: Nevada's summary eviction statutes distinguish between monetary and non-monetary defaults. For nonpayment of rent in a commercial tenancy, NRS 40.2542 governs and requires a notice advising the tenant that it may be evicted at or before noon of the fifth full day (excluding weekends and holidays) following service unless the tenant pays the rent due or files an affidavit with the court contesting the eviction. For non-monetary defaults (e.g., a lease covenant violation), a landlord must proceed under NRS 40.2516, which requires a five-day notice to cure or quit identifying the breach, followed — if the tenant does not cure — by a second notice (a notice to quit for unlawful detainer) directing the tenant to vacate and advising of the right to contest by filing an affidavit with the court. This two-notice structure for non-monetary defaults matches the 2022 baseline's description, though the specific timing (five days, not a generic "notice") is more precisely tied to NRS 40.2516 and 40.2542 for commercial premises specifically (as distinguished from the residential process in NRS 40.253).

sections.heading: Self-Help / Commercial Lockout
sections.text: Nevada continues to permit a form of statutory commercial lockout under NRS 118C.200. A landlord may change the door locks of a commercial tenant delinquent in rent if the landlord gives written notice (by certified mail) of the delinquency and the landlord's intent to change the locks at least three days beforehand, and posts a notice on the front door of the premises identifying where a new key may be obtained during regular business hours (conditioned on payment of overdue rent). A landlord who violates NRS 118C.200 exposes itself to statutory remedies under NRS 118C.210, including recovery of possession or lease termination by the tenant, plus damages of at least one month's rent or $500 (whichever is greater), attorney's fees, and costs, offset by any rent still owed.

sections.heading: Jurisdiction and Venue
sections.text: A "summary" eviction proceeding under NRS 40.2516/40.2542 seeks possession only; a landlord must file a separate plenary action to recover money damages, though it may do so before or after the summary proceeding. Alternatively, a landlord may pursue a "formal" unlawful detainer action combining possession and damages claims in a single suit, with a show-cause hearing available for expedited possession pending trial. These actions are filed in the justice court (or district court for larger claims) in the township/county where the property is located.

sections.heading: Timing
sections.text: A summary eviction hearing on a properly filed tenant affidavit is typically calendared quickly, generally within about a week of the contest being filed, given the five-day notice-and-cure/quit structure. A formal eviction proceeding, by contrast, follows ordinary civil litigation timelines and takes materially longer.

sections.heading: Damages
sections.text: Nevada does not require an acceleration clause to be separately/specially stated to be enforceable, but a landlord does have a duty to mitigate damages upon abandonment. Under NRS 40.360, in an action for forcible entry or unlawful detainer, the court or jury assesses damages occasioned by the wrongful conduct and, where the unlawful detainer follows a rent default, awards the rent due plus treble (three times) the assessed damages against a defendant found guilty of forcible entry or unlawful detainer.

leaseConsiderations: Include an express lockout/self-help notice mechanism consistent with NRS 118C.200 if the landlord wants to preserve that remedy.
Draft default and cure provisions that track the NRS 40.2516 two-notice (cure, then quit) structure for non-monetary defaults.
Include an acceleration clause (not statutorily required, but recommended for clarity).
Address the landlord's mitigation obligations and reletting rights.
Consider whether to pursue summary eviction (possession only, fast) versus formal eviction (combined possession/damages, slower) and draft remedies language accordingly.
Include an attorney's fees provision, as fee-shifting is not automatic outside the treble-damages framework of NRS 40.360.
sourceNotes:
Statutory authorities reviewed: Nev. Rev. Stat. §§ 40.2516, 40.2542, 40.253, 40.360, 118C.200, 118C.210.

sections.heading: Statutory Notice
sections.text: For a nonresidential (commercial) tenant who neglects or refuses to pay rent due and in arrears upon demand, seven days' notice is sufficient. If rent is payable more frequently than once every three months, a notice equal to the rent period is sufficient, and three months' notice is sufficient in all cases. The eviction notice must state with specificity the reason for eviction, and — if based on nonpayment — must inform the tenant of any right to avoid eviction by paying arrearages and liquidated damages under RSA 540:9. N.H. Rev. Stat. Ann. § 540:3.

sections.heading: Self-Help / Commercial Lockout
sections.text: Self-help remedies remain unavailable in New Hampshire; a landlord must proceed through judicial eviction. The statutory penalties for unlawful lockouts and utility shutoffs (RSA 540-A) apply to residential premises, but commercial landlords likewise have no self-help remedy and must obtain a writ through the eviction process to regain possession.

sections.heading: Jurisdiction and Venue
sections.text: Eviction actions are heard in the New Hampshire circuit court (district division). Because money judgments in an eviction proceeding are capped, a landlord will typically need to pursue lease damages beyond that cap in a separate civil action. N.H. Rev. Stat. Ann. § 540:13.

sections.heading: Timing
sections.text: After a writ issues, it is returnable seven days after service, and a tenant has until the return date to file an appearance contesting the eviction. If the tenant appears, the court schedules a hearing within ten days of the appearance being filed. Judgment triggers a seven-day window to note an appeal and thirty days for filing with the New Hampshire Supreme Court. N.H. Rev. Stat. Ann. § 540:13.

sections.heading: Damages
sections.text: Damages are generally governed by the lease terms. New Hampshire law does not clearly establish a landlord's duty to mitigate damages specific to commercial leases, though a general contract-law duty to mitigate exists. Any money judgment awarded within the eviction proceeding itself remains capped, without precluding either party from pursuing additional amounts in a separate action.

sections.heading: Special Considerations
sections.text: The eviction-proceeding money judgment is limited to a maximum of $1,500 and does not preclude either party from bringing a subsequent claim in a court of competent jurisdiction for amounts exceeding that cap. N.H. Rev. Stat. Ann. § 540:13.

sections.heading: 2026 Update Note
sections.text: RSA 540:3 was amended by 2024, ch. 9, § 4, effective January 1, 2025. The amendment restructured the notice provisions to separately address residential (30-day, or 7-day for specified lease violations) and nonresidential/commercial (7-day for nonpayment, tracking the rent-period rule) notice periods, and added the requirement that the eviction notice state with specificity the reason for eviction. Commercial landlords and counsel should confirm their notice forms track the current, more detailed content requirements rather than older short-form notices.

leaseConsiderations: Contractual notice-and-cure provisions, since RSA 540:3's default commercial notice period (7 days for nonpayment) is brief but content requirements are now more detailed.
Explicit statement of reasons in any notice to quit, tracking the current statute's specificity requirement.
Damages/liquidated-damages provisions that anticipate the $1,500 cap on money judgments obtainable within the eviction action itself.
A separate-action reservation clause preserving the landlord's right to pursue full contract damages outside the eviction proceeding.
Mitigation language, given the uncertain state of New Hampshire common law on a landlord's duty to mitigate in commercial leases.
Attorney's fees clause, since fee-shifting is not automatic.
sourceNotes:
Statutory authorities reviewed: N.H. Rev. Stat. Ann. §§ 540:2, 540:3, 540:9, 540:13, 540-A; 2024 N.H. Laws ch. 9, § 4 (amending RSA 540:3), effective January 1, 2025.

sections.heading: Statutory Notice
sections.text: No statutory notice period is required to evict a commercial tenant in default of rent under the Summary Dispossess Act. N.J. Stat. Ann. § 2A:18-53. Written notice to quit is required to remove a commercial holdover tenant. Id. § 2A:18-53. Separately, written notice must be given before disposing of a tenant's abandoned personal property, unless the lease provides otherwise. Id. § 2A:18-72.

sections.heading: Self-Help / Commercial Lockout
sections.text: Self-help remains unavailable as a practical matter for commercial landlords in New Jersey. Recovery of possession must proceed through a summary dispossess action in Superior Court followed by a court-issued warrant of removal executed by a court officer; New Jersey courts have not squarely resolved whether a lease provision expressly authorizing self-help would be enforceable, and practitioners continue to treat self-help as a materially litigation-risky path that should not be relied upon.

sections.heading: Jurisdiction and Venue
sections.text: A summary dispossession action for possession is filed in the Special Civil Part of the Law Division of the Superior Court in the county where the leased premises is located. Possession is the only remedy available in that proceeding; lease damages must be pursued in a separate lawsuit.

sections.heading: Timing
sections.text: Trial in a summary dispossession action is generally scheduled between 10 and 30 days after service of the complaint. After judgment for possession, the landlord must apply for a warrant of removal within 30 days of judgment; the warrant is then executed by a court officer, typically after several days' notice. The overall process commonly takes roughly 60 to 90 days. A separate damages action proceeds on the ordinary civil docket.

sections.heading: Damages
sections.text: Acceleration clauses must be expressly stated in the lease to be enforceable. A landlord has a duty to mitigate damages upon a tenant's breach, and the landlord bears the burden of proving reasonable mitigation efforts.

sections.heading: Special Considerations
sections.text: If a tenant contests the eviction, courts commonly refer the matter to mediation before setting it for trial. Even after judgment for possession, a commercial tenant retains a statutory right to "redeem" the tenancy by paying the rent found owed (as determined by the court or stated in a default judgment certification); a timely redemption permits the tenant to remain. N.J. Stat. Ann. § 2A:18-55. A tenant generally may not appeal a summary dispossession judgment except on jurisdictional grounds. Id. § 2A:18-59.

leaseConsiderations: Express, unambiguous notice-to-quit and cure provisions, since the statute itself imposes no default notice period.
Express acceleration clause, since acceleration is unenforceable absent explicit lease language.
Mitigation and reletting language, given the landlord's statutory mitigation duty and burden of proof.
Redemption-rights awareness in drafting default remedies, since a tenant can redeem even after a possession judgment.
Separate reservation of damages claims, since possession and damages cannot be combined in the summary dispossess proceeding.
Caution against relying on a lease self-help clause given unresolved New Jersey case law.
Attorney's fees provision, since fee-shifting is not automatic.
sourceNotes:
Statutory authorities reviewed: N.J. Stat. Ann. §§ 2A:18-53, 2A:18-55, 2A:18-59, 2A:18-72.

sections.heading: Statutory Notice
sections.text: Three days' written notice to quit must be given before a forcible entry or unlawful detainer action may be filed. N.M. Stat. Ann. § 35-10-3.

sections.heading: Self-Help / Commercial Lockout
sections.text: New Mexico's Uniform Owner-Resident Relations Act, which restricts self-help remedies (e.g., lockouts, utility shutoffs, seizure of personal property), applies only to residential dwelling units and expressly does not govern commercial tenancies. N.M. Stat. Ann. § 47-8-1 et seq. There is no comparable New Mexico statute governing commercial self-help, and secondary authority on the point is inconsistent. Common-law self-help repossession without breach of the peace has historically been treated as legally uncertain and disfavored by New Mexico courts and practitioners given the litigation risk it creates; landlords are generally advised to proceed judicially. ⚠ Could not independently verify with confidence whether New Mexico case law affirmatively forecloses commercial self-help — confirm current status with local counsel before relying on self-help as a remedy.

sections.heading: Jurisdiction and Venue
sections.text: A landlord may recover both possession and damages in a single forcible entry and detainer action. N.M. Stat. Ann. § 35-10-4. The action is filed in the magistrate court or district court for the county where the property is located, but magistrate court jurisdiction is limited to claims of $10,000 or less. Id. § 35-3-3.

sections.heading: Timing
sections.text: The case must be heard within 10 days after service of process on the tenant, though the court may continue the matter for up to 10 additional days.

sections.heading: Damages
sections.text: Rent acceleration clauses are enforceable. New Mexico does not impose a general statutory duty on a commercial landlord to mitigate damages. If the landlord recovers possession and the tenant appeals to district court, the tenant owes the actual rent accrued through the magistrate court judgment, plus double the rent accruing thereafter through entry of judgment in the district court. N.M. Stat. Ann. § 35-10-5.

sections.heading: Special Considerations
sections.text: Where the court finds for the landlord, it customarily awards the rent owed and possession, while allowing the tenant a reasonable period to vacate.

leaseConsiderations: Express acceleration clause to ensure enforceability.
No-mitigation-required language, consistent with the absence of a statutory mitigation duty (subject to any contrary lease terms).
Caution regarding self-help: given the ambiguous legal landscape, an express, carefully limited self-help clause (peaceable re-entry only) is preferable to relying on undefined common-law rights.
Clear default/notice provisions building on (or extending) the bare three-day statutory notice.
Appeal-related rent provisions reflecting the double-rent-on-appeal exposure under § 35-10-5.
Attorney's fees provision, since fee-shifting is not automatic under the forcible entry and detainer statute.
sourceNotes:
Statutory authorities reviewed: N.M. Stat. Ann. §§ 35-3-3, 35-10-3, 35-10-4, 35-10-5, 47-8-1 et seq. (Uniform Owner-Resident Relations Act, residential scope).

sections.heading: Statutory Notice
sections.text: For nonpayment of rent, a landlord must serve a 14-day written rent demand before commencing a nonpayment summary proceeding; the demand must provide a good-faith approximation of the amount owed, the manner in which it may be paid, and the name, address, and contact information of the person to whom payment should be made. N.Y. Real Prop. Acts. Law § 711(2). A holdover proceeding requires a predicate notice terminating the tenancy in accordance with the lease and applicable notice provisions rather than a rent demand.

sections.heading: Self-Help / Commercial Lockout
sections.text: New York continues to recognize limited peaceable self-help re-entry for commercial tenancies at common law, where the right is expressly reserved in the lease. A landlord relying on self-help must reenter without force, threats, or breach of the peace (for example, changing locks without confrontation is more likely to be deemed peaceable, while stationing security guards to physically bar a tenant or threatening to call police on a returning tenant has been held to breach the peace and expose the landlord to liability). Given the litigation risk and fact-specific nature of the peaceable-re-entry standard, judicial eviction remains the more reliable and commonly used path even where a lease authorizes self-help.

sections.heading: Jurisdiction and Venue
sections.text: Damages may be sought together with possession in a summary proceeding. N.Y. Real Prop. Acts. Law § 601. Commercial summary proceedings are heard in the New York City Civil Court (Commercial/Housing Part, by borough), in District Court in certain counties (e.g., Nassau and Suffolk), or in county, city, town, or village courts of appropriate jurisdiction elsewhere in the state. Id. § 701.

sections.heading: Timing
sections.text: After a nonpayment or holdover petition is filed, the notice of petition must be made returnable within a compressed statutory window (generally within about ten days of service, consistent with RPAPL Article 7's expedited summary-proceeding design); if the tenant answers, trial is set on a short timetable. If judgment favors the landlord, the warrant of eviction issues promptly, while a default by the tenant leads to issuance of the warrant on a somewhat longer statutory timeline. N.Y. Real Prop. Acts. Law § 732. Overall, an uncontested case commonly resolves in 30–90 days, while a contested case with defenses or counterclaims can take several months.

sections.heading: Damages
sections.text: New York does not impose a general duty on a commercial landlord to mitigate damages. A rent acceleration clause is enforceable when expressly stated in the lease, though case law continues to scrutinize whether the full accelerated amount is recoverable or instead constitutes an unenforceable penalty, particularly where the landlord has relet the premises and effectively received a windfall. Attorney's fees are recoverable only if expressly provided for in the lease.

leaseConsiderations: Express, precisely drafted rent demand/notice provisions consistent with RPAPL § 711(2)'s content requirements.
Explicit self-help/peaceable re-entry clause if the landlord wishes to preserve that remedy, paired with strict internal protocols to avoid a breach-of-the-peace finding.
Acceleration clause drafted to withstand penalty-clause scrutiny (e.g., present-value discounting, credit for reletting proceeds).
Attorney's fees provision, since fee-shifting is not automatic.
No-mitigation-required language, subject to case-law limits on acceleration recovery.
Clear designation of the proper court/venue for the specific property location given New York's fragmented commercial summary-proceeding jurisdiction.
sourceNotes:
Statutory authorities reviewed: N.Y. Real Prop. Acts. Law §§ 601, 701, 711, 732.

sections.heading: Statutory Notice
sections.text: North Carolina imposes no general statutory notice requirement for commercial evictions where the lease itself addresses default and termination. Where a written or oral lease is silent on when the tenant's right to possession is forfeited for nonpayment, N.C. Gen. Stat. § 42-3 implies a forfeiture of the term if rent is not paid within 10 days after the landlord (or its agent) demands the rent due.

sections.heading: Self-Help / Commercial Lockout
sections.text: Commercial landlords in North Carolina retain a common-law self-help remedy. Under § 42-3, once the implied 10-day forfeiture period following a rent demand has passed (where the lease is silent on the point), the landlord may reenter and dispossess the tenant without first declaring a forfeiture or having reserved a reentry right in the lease — most commonly accomplished by peaceably padlocking the premises. Any reentry must be peaceable; North Carolina courts construe "breach of the peace" broadly, so that virtually any tenant objection at the scene forecloses self-help and leaves summary ejectment through the courts as the landlord's only safe remedy.

sections.heading: Jurisdiction and Venue
sections.text: A landlord may pursue a summary ejectment action seeking possession and damages together, or possession first with damages later. N.C. Gen. Stat. § 42-28. District courts have a $25,000 jurisdictional limit for civil claims generally, which governs the damages a summary ejectment action filed in district court may include. N.C. Gen. Stat. § 7A-243. This corrects the 2022 baseline, which cited a $10,000 limit; that figure was superseded well before the baseline was written — the limit was raised from $10,000 to $25,000 by S.L. 2013-159, effective for actions filed on or after August 1, 2013 — so this is a correction of a stale citation rather than a 2023–2026 change. The action must be filed in the county where the property is located.

sections.heading: Timing
sections.text: After the complaint is filed, the clerk of superior court issues a summons requiring the tenant to appear within a period not exceeding seven days from issuance, excluding weekends and legal holidays. N.C. Gen. Stat. § 42-28. If the tenant fails to appear or is defaulted, the landlord may obtain a writ of possession, which the sheriff must execute within a matter of days of receipt. Id. § 42-36.2.

sections.heading: Damages
sections.text: Rent acceleration clauses are enforceable, but a landlord has a duty to mitigate damages once it regains possession of the premises.

sections.heading: Special Considerations
sections.text: In a summary ejectment action based on nonpayment of rent, the proceeding is stayed or discontinued if the tenant pays or tenders the rent due plus court costs before judgment. N.C. Gen. Stat. § 42-33.

leaseConsiderations: Express default and forfeiture provisions to avoid reliance on the § 42-3 implied 10-day/demand default rule.
Explicit self-help clause reserving the reentry right, understanding that any tenant objection at the scene will likely defeat peaceable self-help.
Rent acceleration clause paired with mitigation/reletting language given the landlord's mitigation duty.
Provisions addressing the interplay between the cure-by-tender right (§ 42-33) and any acceleration remedy the landlord wants to preserve.
Awareness of the $25,000 district-court jurisdictional limit when structuring combined possession/damages claims.
Attorney's fees provision, since fee-shifting is not automatic.
sourceNotes:
Statutory authorities reviewed: N.C. Gen. Stat. §§ 7A-243, 42-3, 42-28, 42-33, 42-36.2; S.L. 2013-159 (raising the district court jurisdictional limit to $25,000, effective August 1, 2013 — a correction to the stale $10,000 figure in the 2022 baseline, not a 2023–2026 change).

sections.heading: Statutory Notice
sections.text: Three days' written notice must be given before an eviction proceeding may be initiated. N.D. Cent. Code Ann. § 47-32-02.

sections.heading: Self-Help / Commercial Lockout
sections.text: Self-help remedies remain unavailable in North Dakota; a landlord must proceed through the statutory eviction action to regain possession.

sections.heading: Jurisdiction and Venue
sections.text: An eviction action for a holdover or material lease breach may be maintained in the appropriate district court, and possession and damages may be awarded in the same proceeding. N.D. Cent. Code Ann. §§ 47-32-01, 47-32-04, 47-16-13.4.

sections.heading: Timing
sections.text: The eviction hearing must be held between three and fifteen days after the eviction action is served on a tenant within the county, or seven to fifteen days for a tenant served outside the county. N.D. Cent. Code Ann. § 47-32-02. Once the court issues an eviction order, the landlord may use it to have the tenant immediately removed, though a tenant may be granted up to five additional days to vacate upon a showing of substantial hardship. Id. § 47-32-04.

sections.heading: Damages
sections.text: An evicted commercial tenant remains liable for rent for the remainder of the lease term, subject to the landlord's duty to mitigate damages. N.D. Cent. Code Ann. § 47-16-13.7. Reasonable attorney's fees are recoverable. Id. § 47-16-13.6.

sections.heading: Special Considerations
sections.text: If a landlord accepts rent after lease expiration, the lease is presumed renewed on the same terms for the same term length, up to one year. N.D. Cent. Code Ann. § 47-16-06. Abandoned property worth less than $2,500 may be kept or disposed of 28 days after the tenant vacates. Id. § 47-16-30.1. Separately, North Dakota enacted a new eviction-record-sealing mechanism (2025 S.B. 2238) allowing a tenant to petition to seal an eviction record seven years after satisfying a judgment for nonpayment or property damage (or immediately in domestic-violence-related cases); this is a court-records/tenant-screening measure rather than a change to the commercial eviction process itself, and does not alter the notice, self-help, jurisdiction, timing, or damages framework above.

leaseConsiderations: Explicit default and notice provisions building on the bare three-day statutory notice.
Mitigation and reletting language, given the landlord's statutory mitigation duty.
Attorney's fees clause, consistent with and reinforcing the statutory fee-shifting right.
Hold-over/renewal language addressing the statutory presumption of renewal upon acceptance of rent after lease expiration.
Abandoned-property disposition provisions coordinated with the 28-day/$2,500 statutory default rule.
No self-help clause reliance, since self-help is unavailable by statute.
sourceNotes:
Statutory authorities reviewed: N.D. Cent. Code Ann. §§ 47-16-06, 47-16-13.4, 47-16-13.6, 47-16-13.7, 47-16-30.1, 47-32-01, 47-32-02, 47-32-04; 2025 N.D. Laws (S.B. 2238, eviction-record sealing, not core to commercial process).

sections.heading: Statutory Notice
sections.text: Three days' statutory notice to leave the premises is required before a forcible entry and detainer action may be filed. Ohio Rev. Code Ann. § 1923.04.

sections.heading: Self-Help / Commercial Lockout
sections.text: Ohio continues to permit commercial self-help repossession at common law, distinct from the residential Landlord-Tenant Act's prohibition on non-judicial evictions. A landlord may use self-help where: the tenant is holding over unlawfully or in breach of the lease; the landlord has given notice of termination or an opportunity to cure; the lease itself provides for self-help repossession; and the repossession is accomplished without a breach of the peace. Ohio courts have reasoned that the legislature's choice to prohibit self-help in residential settings while enacting no comparable prohibition for commercial leases weighs against treating commercial self-help provisions as void on public-policy grounds (see Northfield Park Assocs. v. Northeast Ohio Harness, 36 Ohio App. 3d 14 (Cuyahoga Cty. 1987)).

sections.heading: Jurisdiction and Venue
sections.text: A forcible entry and detainer action may include a claim for damages under the lease, although the court may, for good cause, continue the trial of the damages claim separately from the possession claim. Ohio Rev. Code Ann. § 1923.081.

sections.heading: Timing
sections.text: Most courts schedule a hearing between roughly fourteen and twenty-one days after the complaint is filed. If judgment favors the landlord, the court issues a writ of restitution, which must be executed within ten days of issuance.

sections.heading: Damages
sections.text: A landlord has a duty to mitigate damages. Acceleration clauses are generally enforceable if expressly provided for in the lease agreement.

sections.heading: 2026 Update Note
sections.text: Effective April 9, 2025, Ohio S.B. 237 (135th General Assembly) amended R.C. Chapter 1923, including §§ 1923.01 and 1923.05. The amendments expand forcible entry and detainer grounds to include a tenant financially responsible for, and in default on, municipally provided utility service, and add a protection barring an eviction action from naming a minor tenant as a defendant where a parent or adult guardian is also named, with dismissal and fee-shifting to the minor tenant as a remedy for violation. These changes are directed principally at residential/utility and minor-tenant scenarios and do not materially alter the commercial notice, self-help, jurisdiction, timing, or damages framework described above, but commercial landlords and counsel should be aware the underlying chapter was amended in 2025.

leaseConsiderations: Express self-help clause with notice-and-cure mechanics tracking the Northfield Park factors (termination/cure notice, lease authorization, peaceable execution).
Acceleration clause expressly stated in the lease to ensure enforceability.
Mitigation and reletting language, given the landlord's statutory mitigation duty.
Coordination of possession and damages claims, anticipating that a court may bifurcate and continue the damages portion for good cause.
Attorney's fees provision, since fee-shifting is not automatic outside the narrow minor-tenant-defendant scenario added in 2025.
Contractual notice periods tailored to the business, since three days is a bare statutory minimum.
sourceNotes:
Statutory authorities reviewed: Ohio Rev. Code Ann. §§ 1923.01, 1923.04, 1923.05, 1923.081; Northfield Park Assocs. v. Northeast Ohio Harness, 36 Ohio App. 3d 14, 521 N.E.2d 466 (Cuyahoga Cty. 1987); 2025 Ohio S.B. 237 (135th Gen. Assemb.), effective April 9, 2025.

sections.heading: Statutory Notice
sections.text: No notice to quit is required when the lease specifies a termination date. Okla. Stat. Ann. tit. 41, § 8. Where a tenant neglects or refuses to pay rent due for a period of three months or longer, ten days' written notice to quit is required before the lease is deemed terminated, unless the rent is paid within that period. Id. § 6. A lease provision expressly waiving the requirement of a demand or notice to quit remains enforceable under Oklahoma case law.

sections.heading: Self-Help / Commercial Lockout
sections.text: Self-help remains prohibited in Oklahoma; the statutory forcible entry and detainer procedure is the exclusive method for regaining possession.

sections.heading: Jurisdiction and Venue
sections.text: Claims for collection of rent or property damage may be joined with an action for possession in district court. Okla. Stat. Ann. tit. 12, § 1148.1. The action may proceed on the district court's small claims docket where the amount in controversy does not exceed the small-claims jurisdictional amount ($10,000). Id. §§ 1148.14, 1751. A landlord may instead pursue possession and damages in separate proceedings, and local counsel commonly recommends filing a separate damages action.

sections.heading: Timing
sections.text: After an action is filed, the summons requires the tenant to appear at trial; under 2025 amendments, the summons must generally be served at least seven days before trial (increased from three), with the return day no later than the trial date. Okla. Stat. Ann. tit. 12, § 1148.5. Separately, for actions under Title 41, § 132(C)–(D), the summons period runs not less than five nor more than ten days from issuance. Id. §§ 1148.4, 1148.16. After a writ of possession issues, the tenant receives 48 hours' notice to vacate. Id. § 1148.10A.

sections.heading: Damages
sections.text: Collection of rent, damages to the premises, restitution for unlawful possession by a holdover or forcible-possession tenant, and reasonable attorney's fees may be recovered by the prevailing party. Okla. Stat. Ann. tit. 12 §§ 1148.1, 1148.2, 1148.9. As a general rule, future (unaccrued) rent cannot be collected where the landlord retakes possession, absent contrary lease provision addressing damages.

sections.heading: Special Considerations
sections.text: If a landlord accepts rent after a lease expires, the lease is presumed to have renewed on the same terms and for the same term length, up to one year. Okla. Stat. Ann. tit. 41, § 35. Where a tenant abandons or is evicted and leaves personal property behind, the landlord may take possession of the property 10 days after mailing notice, or 10 days after the tenant is personally served with notice; if the tenant does not reclaim the property or indicate an intent to do so, the landlord may sell it at public sale, subject to the tenant paying all outstanding rent and damages before any return of the property. Id. § 52.

sections.heading: 2026 Update Note
sections.text: Effective November 1, 2025, Oklahoma S.B. 128 amended 12 Okla. Stat. §§ 1148.4, 1148.5, 1148.5A, and 1148.16, principally by extending the minimum period between service of summons and trial from three days to seven days, and by requiring the summons form to be developed in plain, understandable language by the Oklahoma Bar Association. Commercial landlords and counsel should build the longer minimum service-to-trial window into eviction timelines going forward.

leaseConsiderations: Express lease-term-expiration language to avoid triggering the ten-days'-notice-for-nonpayment default rule where a fixed term is intended to control.
Express waiver of demand/notice-to-quit requirements where the landlord wants to shorten the pre-filing runway, consistent with enforceable waiver case law.
Future-rent/liquidated damages provision, since future rent is not recoverable by default upon repossession absent contrary lease language.
Attorney's fees provision, reinforcing the statutory fee-shifting right.
Abandoned-property disposition provisions coordinated with the 10-day notice/public-sale statutory framework.
Awareness of the extended (now seven-day) minimum summons-to-trial period from the 2025 amendment when projecting possession timelines.
Hold-over/renewal language addressing the statutory presumption of renewal upon post-expiration rent acceptance.

sections.heading: Statutory Notice
sections.text: Oregon draws a sharp line between residential and commercial tenancies. For a commercial tenant, no statutory notice to quit is required before a landlord commences a forcible entry and detainer (FED) action for nonpayment of rent — the action may be filed as soon as the tenant fails to pay rent within ten days after it becomes due under the lease (or such other period as the lease specifies). Or. Rev. Stat. §§ 91.090, 105.115(1)(b). Where notice is otherwise required to terminate a commercial tenancy (e.g., for a periodic or holdover tenancy under ORS 91.060–91.080), the tenant may waive that notice by the terms of a written lease. Or. Rev. Stat. § 105.120.

sections.heading: Self-Help / Commercial Lockout
sections.text: Oregon permits peaceable self-help for commercial landlords. Entry to recover possession must be made "in a peaceable manner and without force." Or. Rev. Stat. § 105.105. Oregon courts require that the lease expressly authorize reentry/relocking and that the landlord exercise it without force or breach of the peace; any use of force renders the self-help unlawful.

sections.heading: Jurisdiction and Venue
sections.text: FED actions are tried in the circuit court for the county in which the property is located. Or. Rev. Stat. § 105.110. The action is limited to possession; attorney's fees are rarely awarded in the FED proceeding itself, and damages generally must be pursued in a separate civil action, to be reached on the court's ordinary docket.

sections.heading: Timing
sections.text: After filing, the court sets a status/first appearance conference, typically seven to fifteen days after filing. If the parties do not settle, trial is set roughly seven to fifteen days later. Or. Rev. Stat. § 105.137. No continuance may be granted to a tenant for more than two days unless the tenant provides security for accruing rent, approved by the court. Or. Rev. Stat. § 105.140. Following a landlord's judgment, the court issues a notice of restitution (giving the tenant four days to vacate) and, if needed, a writ of execution directing the sheriff to remove the tenant. Or. Rev. Stat. §§ 105.151, 105.156, 105.161.

sections.heading: Damages
sections.text: Rent-acceleration clauses are enforceable, though courts commonly limit recovery of future rent to roughly three years of damages (highly judge-dependent); a landlord may instead sue periodically for rent as it accrues. Oregon imposes a duty to mitigate damages on the landlord.

sections.heading: Special Considerations
sections.text: Effective January 1, 2026, House Bill 3522 (2025 Or. Laws) allows an owner to use the FED process against squatters with an expedited 24-hour notice procedure. This mechanism targets unauthorized occupants with no lease and does not alter the notice or process rules that apply to a defaulting or holdover commercial tenant under an existing lease.

leaseConsiderations: Express written reentry/relocking authorization to preserve the peaceable self-help remedy.
Contractual waiver of any otherwise-applicable notice period.
Rent-acceleration clause paired with a realistic future-damages cap given judicial reluctance to award more than roughly three years.
Express duty-to-mitigate and reletting provisions.
Attorney's fees provision, since fee-shifting is unlikely to be awarded in the summary FED proceeding itself.
Reservation of the right to pursue damages in a separate action from the possession suit.
Security/surety provisions addressing continuances.
sourceNotes:
Statutory authorities reviewed: Or. Rev. Stat. §§ 91.090, 105.105, 105.110, 105.115, 105.120, 105.137, 105.140, 105.151, 105.156, 105.161; House Bill 3522 (2025 Or. Laws), operative January 1, 2026 (squatter-removal provision).

sections.heading: Statutory Notice
sections.text: A commercial landlord must give ten days' written notice to quit for nonpayment of rent (or use of the premises for an illegal purpose), and thirty days' written notice for other breaches or termination at the end of a term. 68 Pa. Stat. Ann. § 250.501.

sections.heading: Self-Help / Commercial Lockout
sections.text: Pennsylvania is generally counted among the states that prohibit self-help remedies for commercial landlords; recovery of possession must proceed through the magisterial district judge or court process rather than unilateral lockout. The one recognized exception is true abandonment: where a tenant has abandoned the premises, the landlord may re-enter without legal action and either collect rent from the abandoning tenant or relet and sue for any rent deficiency. Separate from possession, Pennsylvania's distraint (levy) statute continues to permit a landlord to seize a tenant's personal property found on the premises for rent due or in arrears, subject to statutory notice, timing (7 a.m.–7 p.m., not Sundays), and procedural requirements. 68 Pa. Stat. Ann. § 250.302. Courts have found aspects of the distress-*sale* process constitutionally infirm as applied in certain circumstances, so landlords should proceed carefully and expect this remedy to be contested if invoked.

sections.heading: Jurisdiction and Venue
sections.text: The magisterial district judge hears commercial landlord-tenant possession actions, and a claim for possession may be combined with a claim for rent/damages in the same proceeding. 68 Pa. Stat. Ann. § 250.503.

sections.heading: Timing
sections.text: Timing is variable, subject to the court's calendar. Id. § 250.503. The tenant must appear within seven to ten days of the date of the summons. Id. § 250.502. A writ of possession may issue upon request after the fifth day following judgment, must be served within forty-eight hours, and is executed on the eleventh day after service. Id. § 250.503.

sections.heading: Damages
sections.text: A landlord may recover damages for unjust detention of the premises plus unpaid rent. Id. § 250.503. As a general rule a landlord must elect between retaking possession and collecting future rent, but accelerated rent may be recovered where (1) the lease so provides and (2) the tenant has abandoned the premises and the landlord has retaken possession — subject to a credit against the judgment for any rent the landlord collects from a replacement tenant. 69 A.3d 642, 656-57 (Pa. Super. 2013).

sections.heading: Special Considerations
sections.text: If a writ of possession issues solely for nonpayment of rent, the tenant may render it ineffective by paying the rent in arrears plus costs. 68 Pa. Stat. Ann. § 250.503. A landlord may dispose of a tenant's abandoned personal property, but must give at least ten days' written notice by first-class mail before doing so (with an additional thirty-day storage option), and faces treble damages, attorney's fees, and costs for noncompliance. Id. § 250.505a.

leaseConsiderations: Explicit notice-and-cure provisions consistent with, or expanding on, the statutory 10-/30-day notice periods.
Express acceleration clause conditioned on abandonment and retaking of possession, with a reletting/mitigation credit mechanism.
Landlord-lien or distraint-related lease language, recognizing that any actual levy must still follow § 250.302's statutory procedure.
Attorney's fees provision, since a possession action may be combined with a rent claim before the magisterial district judge.
Detailed abandoned-property disposal procedures tracking § 250.505a's notice timing to avoid treble-damages exposure.
Non-waiver language addressing post-notice rent acceptance.

sections.heading: Statutory Notice
sections.text: No notice is required before commencing a repossession action for nonpayment; an action may be brought once rent is fifteen days in arrears, whether or not demanded. R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18.1-9 (Commercial Leasing and Other Estates chapter).

sections.heading: Self-Help / Commercial Lockout
sections.text: Self-help is expressly prohibited for commercial leases covered by this chapter, whether purportedly authorized by the common law or by a written or oral lease provision. R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18.1-15.

sections.heading: Jurisdiction and Venue
sections.text: The action for possession is filed in district court, and the court may award judgment for possession together with all rent due and costs in the same proceeding. R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18.1-9.

sections.heading: Timing
sections.text: Under the general forcible entry and detainer statute, a tenant must be served at least six days before trial. R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-19-3. In a commercial nonpayment action under § 34-18.1-9, the tenant must answer within seven days of service, and the case takes precedence on the court's calendar for hearing on the next court day after that period. An issued writ of possession must be executed within twenty days. R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18.1-9.

sections.heading: Damages
sections.text: A landlord may recover all rent due plus costs in the same action. R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18.1-9. Rent-acceleration clauses are enforceable where expressly provided for in the lease, and the parties may expressly disclaim any duty to mitigate by agreement. 182 A.3d 46 (R.I. 2018).

sections.heading: Special Considerations
sections.text: A judgment in a general unlawful detainer action is not appealable. R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-19-8. A judgment in a nonpayment ejectment action under § 34-18.1-9 may be appealed to the superior court, but only within forty-eight hours and only if the tenant pays all rent due. R.I. Gen. Laws §§ 34-18.1-9, 34-18.1-18. Execution of an issued writ may be stayed only if the tenant pays all rent due, and a landlord does not waive its right to possession by accepting such payment. R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-18.1-16.

leaseConsiderations: Express rent-acceleration clause, since it will not be implied.
Express mitigation-disclaimer language if the landlord wants to avoid a duty to mitigate.
Clear default/notice provisions, since the statute itself requires none for a nonpayment action.
Non-waiver language confirming that acceptance of post-filing rent does not waive the right to possession.
Attorney's fees and costs provisions, given the compressed appeal and stay windows.
Contractual notice-and-cure terms for defaults other than nonpayment, which fall outside the fifteen-day/no-notice nonpayment track.

sections.heading: Statutory Notice
sections.text: No notice to quit is required when a tenant fails to pay rent when due, or when a lease term simply expires — the tenancy terminates automatically and the tenant must vacate forthwith. S.C. Code Ann. §§ 27-35-110, 27-35-140.

sections.heading: Self-Help / Commercial Lockout
sections.text: Direct lockout self-help is not a favored remedy in South Carolina; commercial evictions are generally expected to proceed through the magistrate's court. A distinct, court-supervised distraint remedy is available: on abandonment (defined as a tenant's absence for fifteen days after a default in rent payment, S.C. Code Ann. § 27-35-150) or on a rent default generally, a landlord may file an affidavit of rent due (and, if applicable, an affidavit of abandonment) with the magistrate's court and obtain a warrant authorizing seizure and sale of the tenant's property on the premises to satisfy the arrearage; the tenant may halt a sale by posting bond and proceeding to trial. This distraint/distress process is not self-help in the sense of unilateral lockout — it requires a magistrate's court filing and warrant.

sections.heading: Jurisdiction and Venue
sections.text: Circuit courts, county courts, and magistrates have concurrent jurisdiction over ejectment actions, S.C. Code Ann. § 27-33-40, but such actions are typically brought in magistrate's court, where possession and rent owed may be determined in the same proceeding. S.C. Code Ann. § 27-37-155.

sections.heading: Timing
sections.text: The court orders the tenant to vacate or show cause within ten days after service of the order. S.C. Code Ann. § 27-37-20. If the tenant contests, trial proceeds as in any other civil case, id. § 27-37-60, and on motion the magistrate may set the ejectment matter for the next term of court following the tenant's appearance, id. § 27-37-155. After a verdict for the landlord, the magistrate must issue a writ of ejectment within five days, id. § 27-37-100, and the tenant has twenty-four hours to vacate once the writ is executed, id. § 27-37-160.

sections.heading: Damages
sections.text: The tenant must pay rent due and accruing during the ejectment action, and rent continues to accrue after filing so long as the tenant remains in possession. S.C. Code Ann. §§ 27-37-150, 27-37-155. A holdover tenant who remains for three months after a written demand to surrender becomes liable for double the value of use of the premises, recoverable in a separate action. Id. § 27-35-170. A tenant is not liable for future rent once the tenancy is terminated unless the lease expressly provides for recovery of the rent that would have accrued for the remaining term (an enforceable acceleration provision), subject to the landlord's duty to make reasonable efforts to mitigate.

sections.heading: Special Considerations
sections.text: Either party may appeal an ejectment judgment as in any other civil appeal, S.C. Code Ann. § 27-37-120, but an appeal does not stay ejectment unless the tenant posts an appeal bond set by the magistrate, id. § 27-37-130. A landlord does not waive the right to insist on ejectment by accepting rent payments after commencement of the ejectment proceeding. Id. § 27-37-150.

leaseConsiderations: Express acceleration clause, coupled with acknowledgment of the landlord's duty to mitigate.
Express holdover-rent provision (to supplement or exceed the statutory double-value remedy under § 27-35-170).
Non-waiver language for acceptance of post-filing rent.
Drafting the default/abandonment definitions to align with the fifteen-day statutory abandonment trigger under § 27-35-150 if the landlord wants to rely on distraint.
Attorney's fees provision, since none is provided by statute for ejectment.
Appeal-bond and stay provisions addressed contractually where the parties want a different allocation than the statutory default.

sections.heading: Statutory Notice
sections.text: No pre-filing notice to quit is required for nonpayment. Senate Bill 90 (2024 S.D. Sess. Laws, ch. 75), effective July 1, 2024, repealed former SDCL § 21-16-2, which had required three days' written notice to quit before a forcible entry and detainer action could be commenced. A landlord may now file a forcible entry and detainer action directly once a statutory default (e.g., failure to pay rent) exists, subject to any contrary notice provision the parties have written into the lease.

sections.heading: Self-Help / Commercial Lockout
sections.text: No South Dakota statute prohibits commercial self-help; the common-law remedy may still be available. However, if a landlord wrongfully and forcibly ejects or excludes a tenant from rightful possession, the landlord may be liable for treble the tenant's actual damages. S.D. Codified Laws § 21-3-6.

sections.heading: Jurisdiction and Venue
sections.text: Circuit court or magistrate court has jurisdiction over a forcible entry and detainer action concerning property in its county. S.D. Codified Laws § 21-16-3. Claims for rent and damages may be joined with the possession action, or possession and damages may be pursued in separate actions. Id. § 21-16-4.

sections.heading: Timing
sections.text: The tenant must now appear and plead within five days after service (increased from the former four-day period by SB 90's amendment of SDCL § 21-16-7), and the court may not adjourn or continue the action for more than fourteen days unless the tenant provides "good and sufficient surety" covering rent that may accrue and damages the tenant may owe if judgment goes against him. S.D. Codified Laws § 21-16-7. The action may be brought to trial "upon two days' notice after issue is joined." Id. § 21-16-8.

sections.heading: Damages
sections.text: Rents, profits, damages, costs, and attorney's fees may be recovered, id. §§ 21-16-10, 21-16-11, although attorney's fees for the damages portion of the case are recoverable only if the lease expressly provides for them. A tenant who willfully holds over after notice to quit and demand for possession is liable for double rent thereafter, id. § 21-3-8, as is a tenant who fails to surrender possession after giving notice of intent to do so, id. § 21-3-7. South Dakota has not definitively resolved whether a landlord owes a duty to mitigate, though a landlord may at least decline to relet to an unsuitable replacement tenant. 800 N.W.2d 730 (S.D. 2011).

sections.heading: Special Considerations
sections.text: If a landlord accepts rent after lease expiration, the lease is presumed to renew on the same terms for the same term length, up to one year. S.D. Codified Laws § 43-32-14.

sections.heading: 2026 Update Note
sections.text: Effective July 1, 2024, Senate Bill 90 (2024 S.D. Sess. Laws, ch. 75) repealed the three-day statutory notice-to-quit requirement of former SDCL § 21-16-2 and amended SDCL § 21-16-7 to extend the tenant's appearance period from four to five days after service, streamlining the front end of the eviction timeline for South Dakota landlords.

leaseConsiderations: Contractual notice-and-cure provisions, since the statutory pre-filing notice requirement no longer exists as a floor.
Express acceleration and holdover double-rent provisions to supplement §§ 21-3-7 and 21-3-8.
Attorney's fees clause covering the damages portion of any combined possession/rent action.
Self-help/reentry language addressing peaceable-manner limits, given the treble-damages exposure under § 21-3-6 for wrongful forcible exclusion.
Express duty-to-mitigate (or disclaimer) language, since South Dakota case law has not settled the question.
Renewal/holdover-acceptance language to override the automatic one-year-renewal presumption under § 43-32-14 if not desired.
sourceNotes:
Statutory authorities reviewed: S.D. Codified Laws §§ 21-3-6, 21-3-7, 21-3-8, 21-16-3, 21-16-4, 21-16-7, 21-16-8, 21-16-10, 21-16-11, 43-32-14; Senate Bill 90, 2024 S.D. Sess. Laws, ch. 75, effective July 1, 2024; 800 N.W.2d 730 (S.D. 2011) (mitigation).
