sections.heading: Statutory Notice
sections.text: No statutory notice to quit is required before filing a forcible entry and detainer action; the detainer warrant itself serves as notice. Tenn. Code Ann. § 29-18-113.

sections.heading: Self-Help / Commercial Lockout
sections.text: Self-help is prohibited in Tennessee; landlords must obtain possession through the judicial forcible entry and detainer process rather than by unilateral lockout, subject to a narrow exception for true abandonment or voluntary surrender.

sections.heading: Jurisdiction and Venue
sections.text: A forcible detainer action may be brought in the circuit court or the court of general sessions for the county where the property is located. Tenn. Code Ann. §§ 29-18-107, 29-18-108. Damages are assessed as part of the possession action. Id. §§ 29-18-120, 29-18-125.

sections.heading: Timing
sections.text: Trial may not be set less than six days from the date the tenant is served with the detainer warrant. Tenn. Code Ann. § 29-18-117. The trial date may be extended, by either party, up to fifteen days (or longer by agreement). Id. § 29-18-118. Circuit court actions go to trial on the first term after the pleadings close. Id. § 29-18-120. A writ of possession may not issue sooner than ten days after judgment, id. § 29-18-126, and the sheriff has twenty days to execute and return the writ, id. § 29-18-127.

sections.heading: Damages
sections.text: Damages for breach of a commercial lease should place the landlord in the position it would have occupied absent the breach, subject to the landlord's duty to mitigate; the tenant bears the burden of proving the landlord failed to exercise reasonable care and diligence in mitigating. Acceleration clauses and attorney's fees provisions are enforceable where set forth in the lease.

sections.heading: Special Considerations
sections.text: A tenant has ten days to appeal. Tenn. Code Ann. § 29-18-128. An eviction action in general sessions court is tried by the judge without a jury. Id. § 29-18-107. Before a writ may issue, the landlord must post bond covering costs and damages that may accrue to the tenant for wrongful prosecution. Id. § 29-18-111.

sections.heading: 2026 Update Note
sections.text: Effective July 1, 2025, Public Chapter 90 (2025) (S.B. 292/H.B. 216) amended Tenn. Code Ann. Titles 29 and 66 to create an expedited procedure — a verified "Complaint to Remove Persons Unlawfully Occupying Commercial Real Property," submitted to the county sheriff — for commercial property owners to remove squatters and other unauthorized occupants of vacant commercial real estate. This new procedure applies only to occupants with no valid lease; a tenant holding under a signed commercial lease remains subject to, and protected by, the standard forcible entry and detainer process described above.

leaseConsiderations: Express acceleration clause and attorney's fees provision, since neither is implied by statute.
Mitigation-standard language allocating the burden of proof consistent with (or varying) the default rule placing that burden on the tenant.
Contractual notice-and-cure terms, since none is required by statute before filing.
Bond/security provisions addressing the landlord's statutory obligation to post bond before a writ issues.
Jury-trial waiver language for any circuit court proceeding, since general sessions actions are already tried without a jury.
Provisions distinguishing lease-based default remedies from the new Public Chapter 90 unauthorized-occupant procedure, to avoid inadvertently treating a defaulting tenant as an unlawful occupant.

classificationNote: Chapter 93 lockout rights and a functioning summary-disposition procedure continue to give Texas landlords faster, lower-cost paths to possession than most jurisdictions.

sections.heading: Statutory Notice
sections.text: Unless the parties have contracted for a shorter or longer notice period in a written lease or agreement, a landlord must give a tenant who defaults or holds over beyond the end of the rental term or renewal period at least three days' written notice to vacate before filing a forcible detainer suit. Beginning January 1, 2026, Texas Property Code § 24.005 distinguishes certain nonpayment actions by requiring a notice to pay rent or vacate when the tenant's right of possession is terminated solely for nonpayment of rent and the tenant was not delinquent before the month in which the notice was given. Section 24.005 also specifies approved notice-delivery methods, including mail, delivery inside the premises in a conspicuous place, hand delivery to a tenant age 16 or older, and approved electronic delivery where agreed in writing.

sections.heading: Self-Help / Commercial Lockout
sections.text: Texas continues to permit commercial lockouts under Chapter 93 of the Texas Property Code. A commercial landlord may change the door locks of a tenant who is delinquent in paying at least part of the rent. However, the landlord may not intentionally exclude a commercial tenant except by judicial process unless the exclusion results from bona fide repairs, construction, an emergency, abandonment, or a lockout authorized by § 93.002. The landlord must post written notice on the tenant’s front door identifying the person or company from which a new key may be obtained. Chapter 93 also provides a statutory reentry remedy if a tenant is unlawfully locked out.

sections.heading: Commercial Tenant Reentry
sections.text: If a commercial tenant is locked out in violation of § 93.002, the tenant may file a sworn complaint for reentry in the justice court where the premises are located. The court may issue an ex parte writ of reentry granting temporary possession pending a final hearing if the court reasonably believes an unlawful lockout likely occurred. A writ of possession supersedes a writ of reentry.

sections.heading: Jurisdiction and Venue
sections.text: A justice court in the precinct where the leased premises are located has jurisdiction over eviction proceedings, and the eviction action must be filed in that precinct. The justice court adjudicates possession rights but does not determine title disputes. Counterclaims and third-party claims are not permitted in the eviction action and must be asserted separately.

sections.heading: Possession Procedure
sections.text: For eviction actions filed on or after January 1, 2026, Rule 510 governs eviction proceedings. Texas law now authorizes summary disposition procedures in specified forcible entry and detainer actions where no genuine dispute of material fact exists. A landlord may file a sworn motion for summary disposition together with the petition and obtain judgment without trial unless the tenant timely demonstrates the existence of a genuine factual dispute.

sections.heading: Timing
sections.text: Service of the citation and petition generally must be attempted within five business days after filing. Trial must occur no earlier than the tenth day and no later than the twenty-first day after the petition is filed, may not occur earlier than the fourth day after service on the tenant, and may not be postponed more than seven days absent written agreement of the parties.

sections.heading: Damages
sections.text: Texas continues to recognize acceleration provisions when properly drafted and continues to impose a duty to mitigate damages following abandonment of leased premises. Unpaid rent claims may be joined in the eviction action where permitted by Rule 510. Landlords should preserve future-rent remedies, acceleration rights, attorney-fee provisions, and post-possession damage claims in the lease documents.

sections.heading: 2026 Update Note
sections.text: Effective January 1, 2026, Chapter 24 of the Texas Property Code and Rule 510 underwent substantial revision through S.B. 38. The amendments address notice content, delivery methods, venue, computation of time, service requirements, summary disposition procedures, trial timing, and appellate procedures. Commercial landlords should ensure that all notices, lease forms, and eviction procedures are reviewed for compliance with the revised statutory framework.

leaseConsiderations: Express acceleration clause.
Attorney’s fees provision.
Survival of damages after repossession.
Contractual notice periods.
Electronic notice authorization.
Commercial lockout procedures.
Mitigation language.
Reservation of separate damages claims.

Docket No. 25-9105, dated December 31, 2025.

sections.heading: Statutory Notice
sections.text: Utah requires three days' written notice before an unlawful detainer action based on nonpayment of rent may proceed, and notice may be served any time after rent becomes due. Utah Code Ann. § 78B-6-802(1)(c).

sections.heading: Self-Help / Commercial Lockout
sections.text: Contrary to the 2022 baseline, Utah law does prohibit self-help exclusion of a tenant: it is unlawful for an owner to willfully exclude a tenant from the premises "in any manner except by judicial process." Utah Code Ann. § 78B-6-814. The statute carves out an abandonment exception — the landlord may retake and attempt to relet premises, and may remove the contents, once the premises are abandoned (presumed, among other things, where the tenant fails to notify the owner of an absence and fails to pay rent within fifteen days of the due date with no other reasonable evidence of continued occupancy). Id. §§ 78B-6-814, 78B-6-816. Section 78B-6-814 is not limited to residential tenancies and applies to commercial leases as well.

sections.heading: Jurisdiction and Venue
sections.text: A plaintiff may claim damages, compensation for occupation of the premises, or both, in the same unlawful detainer action. Utah Code Ann. § 78B-6-807(1)(c).

sections.heading: Timing
sections.text: A defendant must appear within three business days of service unless the defendant objects and the court finds more time warranted. Id. § 78B-6-807(3)(a). If the tenant remains in possession, the court must expedite proceedings and begin trial within sixty days of service of the complaint absent agreement otherwise. Id. § 78B-6-810(1). On request of either party, the court must hold an evidentiary hearing within ten business days after the answer or response to determine occupancy rights pending litigation, and may enter final judgment at that hearing if all issues can be adjudicated without further proceedings. Id. § 78B-6-810(2).

sections.heading: Damages
sections.text: A plaintiff may recover damages from forcible entry, forcible or unlawful detainer, waste (if alleged and proved), amounts due under the contract, and abatement of a nuisance, where applicable. Id. § 78B-6-811(2). Judgment against a losing defendant includes rent, three times the assessed damages, costs, and reasonable attorney's fees. Id. § 78B-6-811(3), (5). Utah applies a "retained jurisdiction" approach for future rent, under which the court retains jurisdiction over the parties and subject matter and may enter supplemental damage awards as additional rent accrues, based on past events and taking the landlord's mitigation efforts into account. 776 P.2d 896, 908 (Utah 1989).

leaseConsiderations: Do not rely on self-help/lockout language as a stand-alone remedy; Utah requires judicial process except in a defined abandonment scenario.
Precisely defined abandonment provisions tracking the statutory presumption under § 78B-6-814/816 if the landlord wants to invoke the self-help exception.
Acceleration clause paired with mitigation language, given the retained-jurisdiction approach to future rent.
Attorney's fees provision (though the statute already provides fee-shifting in unlawful detainer judgments, express lease language avoids ambiguity).
Notice-and-cure provisions consistent with, or extending, the three-day statutory floor.
Provisions addressing the treble-damages exposure under § 78B-6-811 for a losing tenant.
sourceNotes:
Statutory authorities reviewed: Utah Code Ann. §§ 78B-6-802, 78B-6-807, 78B-6-810, 78B-6-811, 78B-6-814, 78B-6-816; 776 P.2d 896 (Utah 1989) (retained-jurisdiction approach to future rent).

sections.heading: Statutory Notice
sections.text: Vermont does not require a commercial landlord to give a notice of default unless the lease itself requires one.

sections.heading: Self-Help / Commercial Lockout
sections.text: No Vermont statute prohibits a commercial landlord from using self-help remedies, provided they are exercised in a peaceable manner. Vt. Stat. Ann. tit. 12, § 4911 (entry must not be made "with strong hand or multitude of people," but only peaceably).

sections.heading: Jurisdiction and Venue
sections.text: Entry and detainer actions proceed under Title 12, Chapter 171 of the Vermont Statutes. A landlord may recover treble damages beginning at the time notice to quit is delivered to the tenant; before notice is given, only actual damages are recoverable in a separate trespass action. Vt. Stat. Ann. tit. 12, § 4923.

sections.heading: Timing
sections.text: No specific statutory timeline governs the pace of a Vermont commercial eviction action; timing is variable and depends on the general civil docket.

sections.heading: Damages
sections.text: A prevailing party may recover court costs and a nominal fine not to exceed $10, in the court's discretion. Vt. Stat. Ann. tit. 12, §§ 4916, 4917. Treble damages are available, accruing from the time notice to quit is given. Id. § 4923. A commercial landlord has a duty to mitigate when a tenant abandons the premises, though this duty does not relieve the tenant of its existing lease obligation to pay rent, and a landlord is not required to accept a tenant's attempted surrender. 648 A.2d 1374, 1376-77 (Vt. 1994).

sections.heading: Special Considerations
sections.text: A 2026 legislative effort (S.309/H.772, which would have added a "just cause" ejectment framework and confidentiality provisions to Title 12, Chapter 169) failed on the Senate floor in May 2026 after a 15-15 tie vote, so it did not become law; current commercial ejectment/entry-and-detainer procedure is unchanged from the pre-existing statutory scheme described above.

leaseConsiderations: Express default-notice provisions, since none is required by statute.
Express self-help/reentry authorization confirming peaceable-manner limits under § 4911.
Acceleration clause language, since Vermont's default remedy structure (nominal statutory damages plus treble damages tied to notice) does not itself provide for future-rent recovery.
Mitigation and non-acceptance-of-surrender language tracking Vermont case law.
Contractual timing/procedure provisions (expedited notice-and-cure, arbitration, or similar), given the absence of a statutory eviction timeline.
Monitor future legislative sessions, since comprehensive landlord-tenant reform efforts have recently come close to passage.
sourceNotes:
Statutory authorities reviewed: Vt. Stat. Ann. tit. 12, §§ 4911, 4916, 4917, 4923; 648 A.2d 1374 (Vt. 1994) (mitigation/surrender); S.309 and H.772 (2026 Vt. biennium, introduced but not enacted).

sections.heading: Statutory Notice
sections.text: A commercial landlord may proceed to recover possession after giving five days' written notice for failure to pay rent; the tenant forfeits the right of possession if the default continues for five days after receipt of the notice. Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1415.

sections.heading: Self-Help / Commercial Lockout
sections.text: Self-help eviction remains available to a commercial (nonresidential) landlord without further legal process, so long as it does not incite a breach of the peace. Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1415. Nothing in the statute precludes the landlord from instead pursuing an unlawful detainer action under Article 13 of Title 8.01. In practice, landlords commonly exercise self-help by relocking premises while the tenant's business is closed and unoccupied, to minimize breach-of-the-peace risk.

sections.heading: Jurisdiction and Venue
sections.text: Jurisdiction lies with either the circuit court or the general district court. Va. Code Ann. §§ 8.01-124, 8.01-126. A suit for possession may be combined with a suit for damages and rent owed. Id. § 8.01-128.

sections.heading: Timing
sections.text: Repossession — whether by self-help or legal process — may begin once the tenant is five days in default following written notice. Id. § 55.1-1415. Unlawful detainer actions are generally handled like other civil jury trials, id. § 8.01-125, but the plaintiff may request bifurcation: a final, appealable judgment for possession at the initial hearing on the unlawful detainer summons, with a continuance date set no later than 120 days from that hearing to determine final rent and damages. Id. § 8.01-128. If the defendant contests the amount of rent and damages at the initial hearing, the court will not bifurcate the case.

sections.heading: Damages
sections.text: Damages sustained from unlawful possession, together with any rent owed, may be recovered. Id. § 8.01-128(A). Virginia recognizes the validity of acceleration clauses in commercial leases, but such a clause may be an unenforceable penalty if grossly disproportionate to actual damages. 1996 WL 1065475, at *2 (Va. Cir. Ct. 1996).

sections.heading: Special Considerations
sections.text: Many Virginia landlord-tenant provisions include "unless the lease provides otherwise" language, and Virginia courts broadly respect the parties' freedom to contract around the Code's default provisions, particularly where the contract grants the parties greater rights than the statute provides.

sections.heading: 2026 Update Note
sections.text: Effective July 1, 2024, amendments to Va. Code Ann. § 8.01-128 clarified and codified the bifurcation procedure described above — allowing a plaintiff to obtain a final, appealable possession judgment at the initial hearing while continuing the rent/damages determination for up to 120 days — and specified that the court will not bifurcate if the defendant contests the rent and damages amount at that initial hearing. Commercial landlords and counsel should confirm the current pleading-form requirements (including requesting all amounts due as of the hearing date, plus an approximation of amounts coming due) reflect this codified procedure.

leaseConsiderations: Express self-help/reentry provisions, since Virginia remains one of the minority of states permitting peaceable commercial self-help.
Acceleration clause drafted to avoid characterization as an unenforceable penalty (i.e., reasonably related to anticipated damages).
Contractual notice periods that expand on, or otherwise supersede, the five-day statutory floor where the parties prefer a different standard.
Bifurcation-aware drafting: attorney's fees and rent-acceleration provisions that will support a strong damages case within the 120-day continuance window.
Non-waiver language for acceptance of rent following notice or filing.
Explicit "lease provides otherwise" drafting wherever the parties want to displace a Code default rule, given Virginia courts' willingness to enforce such contractual variations.
sourceNotes: Statutory authorities reviewed: Va. Code Ann. §§ 8.01-124, 8.01-125, 8.01-126, 8.01-128, 55.1-1415; 1996 WL 1065475 (Va. Cir. Ct. 1996) (acceleration-clause penalty doctrine); 2024 amendments to § 8.01-128 (bifurcation procedure), effective July 1, 2024.

sections.heading: Statutory Notice
sections.text: Washington does not require pre-suit notice as a general matter before a commercial landlord may commence an unlawful detainer action for most defaults, but a specific notice is required for nonpayment of rent. Where a tenant continues in possession after defaulting on rent, the landlord must serve a written notice, in the alternative, demanding payment of the rent or surrender of the premises; the tenant has three days after service to comply (fourteen days applies only to tenancies governed by the Residential Landlord-Tenant Act, chapter 59.18 RCW, which does not apply to commercial tenancies). Wash. Rev. Code Ann. § 59.12.030(3). The notice may be served at any time after rent becomes due. Service methods, proof of service, and required notice content are governed by RCW 59.12.040.

sections.heading: Self-Help / Commercial Lockout
sections.text: Washington courts have long disfavored landlord self-help and require landlords to regain possession through the judicial unlawful detainer process rather than by forcible reentry, lockout, or exclusion, reflecting the state's longstanding policy — reflected as early as *Barnes v. Bickle*, 111 Wash. 133, 189 P. 998 (1920) — that a tenant's right to exclusive possession may not be interfered with by unauthorized landlord entry. While Chapter 59.12 does not contain an express statutory prohibition on commercial self-help comparable to RCW 59.18.290 (which applies only to residential tenancies under chapter 59.18 RCW), commercial landlords should not rely on self-help remedies even where a lease purports to authorize them; courts construe such lease language narrowly and against the landlord, and self-help exposes a landlord to trespass and conversion liability.

sections.heading: Jurisdiction and Venue
sections.text: The superior court of the county in which the property is located has jurisdiction over unlawful detainer actions. Wash. Rev. Code Ann. § 59.12.050. A claim for damages and rent may be combined with the claim for possession in the same action. Id. § 59.12.170.

sections.heading: Timing
sections.text: Timing is variable. After the complaint and summons are filed, the summons must set a return date not less than seven nor more than thirty days from the date of service, and the complaint must state the amount of rent claimed. Id. § 59.12.070. The plaintiff may apply for a writ of restitution at the time of filing or at any time thereafter, but the defendant may stay execution by posting a bond. Id. §§ 59.12.090, 59.12.100. The action proceeds as a jury trial unless waived, and unlawful detainer actions take precedence over other civil actions on the docket. Id. § 59.12.130.

sections.heading: Damages
sections.text: The jury (or the court in a bench trial) assesses damages resulting from the unlawful detainer as alleged and proved, together with any rent found due, and judgment is entered for twice that combined amount. Id. § 59.12.170. A defendant may reinstate the tenancy by paying the full judgment amount, including costs, within five days after entry of judgment. Id. An acceleration-of-rent clause is enforceable where the lease unequivocally makes the tenant liable for unpaid rent even after lease termination and landlord reentry, and a landlord has a duty to mitigate by re-leasing the premises unless the lease specifically relieves it of that duty.

sections.heading: 2026 Update Note
sections.text: Effective June 11, 2026, House Bill 2664 (Chapter 144, Laws of 2026) amended RCW 59.12.040 to remove the certified-mail requirement for substitute service of unlawful detainer and related notices that had been imposed by 2025 legislation (2025 c 44, based on HB 1003). Under the current version, when a notice cannot be served personally and is instead left with a person of suitable age at the premises, a copy may again be sent by ordinary first-class mail rather than certified mail; mailed service is still deemed complete upon deposit in the mail from within Washington, postage prepaid, and adds five days before an action may be commenced.

leaseConsiderations: Express, narrowly drawn default and cure notice provisions specifying delivery method and cure period, since courts construe ambiguous lease language against the landlord as drafter.
Do not rely on lease "self-help" or lockout clauses as a substitute for the statutory unlawful detainer process.
Express acceleration clause tied unequivocally to tenant liability post-termination and post-reentry.
Mitigation language allocating (or expressly disclaiming) the landlord's duty to re-lease.
Non-waiver provisions addressing acceptance of partial or late rent payments, which can waive termination rights.
Contractual notice-period and delivery-method provisions consistent with RCW 59.12.040's current mailing rules.
Attorney's fees provision, since Washington does not provide a general statutory right to fees in commercial unlawful detainer actions absent lease or other statutory authority.
Reservation of separate damages claims and rent/possession joinder language consistent with RCW 59.12.170.

sections.heading: Statutory Notice
sections.text: West Virginia statute does not impose a generally applicable pre-suit notice period for a commercial unlawful detainer action based on nonpayment of rent or breach of covenant; a landlord with a right of reentry may proceed by serving a declaration in ejectment or commencing an unlawful detainer action once rent is due and unpaid or a covenant has been breached, without a separate statutory notice-and-cure period. W. Va. Code Ann. § 37-6-19. This differs from the abandonment-specific procedure discussed below, which does require notice. Commercial landlords remain free to (and typically do) contract for a notice-and-cure period in the lease itself.

sections.heading: Self-Help / Commercial Lockout
sections.text: Self-help is available to a West Virginia commercial landlord only in defined circumstances, not as a general remedy for a tenant who remains in possession while in default. Where a tenant in arrears has abandoned the leased property, the landlord may post notice on the premises requiring payment of the rent in arrears within one month; if the rent remains unpaid, the landlord is entitled to take possession without judicial process. Id. § 37-6-6(a). Outside of this abandonment scenario, West Virginia does not have a general commercial self-help statute, and landlords should not assume that lockout or exclusion is available against a tenant who remains in occupancy.

sections.heading: Jurisdiction and Venue
sections.text: A claim for damages arising from the unlawful detainer may be assessed in the same proceeding as the claim for possession. Id. §§ 55-3-2, 55-3-4.

sections.heading: Timing
sections.text: Timing is variable. A summons must be returnable not more than ninety days after its date and served at least ten days before the return date; the case proceeds to a jury trial on a "not guilty" plea (or upon default), and the action takes precedence over all other civil causes on the docket. Id. § 55-3-3.

sections.heading: Damages
sections.text: Recoverable damages may include mesne profits of the premises for a period not exceeding three years before commencement of the action, special damages resulting from the unlawful detainer, and damages for destruction or waste of the property. Id. § 55-3-2. Interest on rent is recoverable as on other contracts. Id. § 37-6-9. In the abandonment scenario described above, the landlord may recover rent owed up through the date it became entitled to possession. Id. § 37-6-6(a). More generally, "[r]ent of every kind may be recovered by distress or action." Id. § 37-6-9. A landlord has the option, but not the obligation, to relet the premises after regaining possession; if it does so, the original tenant remains liable for the difference between the rent received from the new tenant and the rent owed under the original lease. Id. § 37-6-7.

leaseConsiderations: Contractual notice-and-cure provisions, since West Virginia statute does not impose a default notice period outside the abandonment context.
Express acceleration clause, since no general statutory acceleration remedy exists.
Mitigation/reletting language clarifying the landlord's optional right (not duty) to relet and the tenant's continuing liability for any deficiency under § 37-6-7.
Distress and self-help limitations — do not assume lockout rights outside of the narrow abandonment procedure in § 37-6-6(a); require judicial process for occupied defaults.
Interest and late-fee provisions to supplement the general statutory interest allowance under § 37-6-9.
Attorney's fees provision, since West Virginia does not provide a general statutory right to fees in commercial unlawful detainer actions.
Damages-period language addressing the three-year mesne-profits limitation in § 55-3-2.

Statutory authorities reviewed: W. Va. Code Ann. §§ 37-6-6, 37-6-7, 37-6-9, 37-6-19, 37-6-30, 55-3-2, 55-3-3, 55-3-4; W. Va. Code Ann. § 55-3A-1 et seq. (Remedies for Wrongful Occupation of Residential Rental Property — confirmed residential-only and excluded from this commercial analysis). No 2023–2026 amendment to these commercial-eviction provisions was identified in this research; the 2022 baseline substance remains current.

sections.heading: Statutory Notice
sections.text: Notice requirements under Chapter 704 (Landlord and Tenant), which applies to commercial as well as residential tenancies, depend on lease duration and the nature of the default. For a lease of more than one year, if the tenant fails to pay rent when due, commits waste, or breaches any other covenant or condition, the tenancy is terminated only if the landlord gives written notice requiring the tenant to pay the rent, repair the waste, or otherwise comply on or before a date at least thirty days after the notice is given, and the tenant fails to comply. Wis. Stat. Ann. § 704.17(3). Shorter cure periods (generally five or fourteen days) apply to month-to-month, year-to-year, and sub-one-year leases under § 704.17(1p) and (2).

sections.heading: Self-Help / Commercial Lockout
sections.text: No Wisconsin statute categorically prohibits a commercial landlord from using self-help remedies, and commercial tenancies are not covered by the residential lockout and rental-practices protections that apply to dwelling units. Commercial landlords should nonetheless proceed cautiously, since any lockout carries a real risk of tort liability (e.g., conversion, breach of the covenant of quiet enjoyment) if executed without clear lease authorization or if it breaches the peace.

sections.heading: Jurisdiction and Venue
sections.text: Small-claims procedure under Chapter 799 is the exclusive procedure for eviction actions, regardless of the amount of rent claimed. Id. § 799.01(1)(a). A landlord may join with the claim for restitution of the premises any other claim against the defendant arising out of the defendant's possession or occupancy. Id. § 799.40(2).

sections.heading: Timing
sections.text: In eviction actions, the summons return date for a defendant served within Wisconsin must be no less than five nor more than twenty-five days after the issue date; if the defendant is not a Wisconsin resident, the return date must be no less than twenty days after issuance. Id. § 799.05. Overall timing otherwise varies by county calendar.

sections.heading: Damages
sections.text: At minimum, a landlord may recover twice the rental value, apportioned daily, for the period the tenant remains in possession after being required to vacate — "rental value" being the amount for which the premises might reasonably have been rented, but not less than the amount actually paid or payable for the prior rental period (including allocable taxes, insurance, and repair costs). Id. § 704.27. A landlord may recover more upon proof of greater actual damages, and may pursue any other available remedy. Wisconsin case law holds that once a landlord successfully re-leases the premises, the original tenant is released from further rent liability, with any rent received from the successor tenant credited against the original tenant's obligation. 624 N.W.2d 847, 850 (Wis. 2001) (case name not independently re-verified in this research; cited consistent with the 2022 baseline — ⚠ confirm case name and current validity with counsel before relying on this citation in isolation).

sections.heading: 2026 Update Note
sections.text: 2025 Wisconsin Act 105 amended Wis. Stat. § 799.01(1)(c)–(d) to raise the general small-claims/circuit-court monetary jurisdiction threshold from $10,000 to $15,000, effective January 1, 2027. Because any non-possessory damages claim joined with an eviction action under § 799.40(2) is subject to this general small-claims jurisdictional ceiling, the increase will expand the size of a damages claim a landlord may join with a Chapter 799 eviction action once effective; larger claims must still be pursued separately in circuit court under ordinary civil procedure. The dedicated eviction-possession claim itself remains unlimited in dollar amount under § 799.01(1)(a).

leaseConsiderations: Express cure-period provisions tailored to lease term, since statutory cure periods scale with lease duration (5, 14, or 30 days).
Acceleration-of-rent clause, since Wisconsin's minimum statutory holdover damages (double daily rental value) may understate actual landlord losses.
Mitigation/reletting language addressing when and how re-letting releases the original tenant, consistent with Wisconsin case law crediting successor rent against the original tenant's liability.
Self-help caution clause — even though not statutorily prohibited for commercial premises, specify peaceable, narrowly conditioned lockout procedures to reduce tort exposure.
Attorney's fees provision, since Wisconsin does not provide a general statutory right to fees in commercial eviction actions.
Joinder-of-claims language anticipating the small-claims monetary ceiling applicable to damages claims joined with possession under § 799.40.
Rental-value definition provision to avoid disputes over the § 704.27 statutory minimum-damages calculation.

Statutory authorities reviewed: Wis. Stat. Ann. §§ 704.01, 704.17, 704.27, 799.01, 799.05, 799.40; 2025 Wisconsin Act 105 (effective January 1, 2027, amending § 799.01(1)(c)–(d) monetary jurisdiction); 2025 Wisconsin Act 247 (technical/session updates incorporated into current statute text, no substantive commercial-eviction change identified); 624 N.W.2d 847 (Wis. 2001), carried forward from the 2022 baseline for the reletting/release rule (case name not independently re-verified — see ⚠ note above). sections.heading: Statutory Notice
sections.text: A commercial tenant must be personally served with written notice at least three days before a forcible entry and detainer action may be commenced. Wyo. Stat. Ann. § 1-21-1003.

sections.heading: Self-Help / Commercial Lockout
sections.text: No Wyoming statute or reported decision expressly forbids a commercial landlord from using self-help remedies, so a common-law self-help remedy may remain available in principle; however, in practice landlords face meaningful risk of liability (including for breach of the peace or wrongful exclusion) absent clear lease authorization, and the statutory forcible entry and detainer process under Article 10 remains the standard and safer path to possession.

sections.heading: Jurisdiction and Venue
sections.text: Circuit courts have jurisdiction over forcible entry and detainer actions. Wyo. Stat. Ann. § 1-21-1001. General circuit court civil jurisdiction (which governs a damages claim joined with a possession claim) extends to matters not exceeding $50,000, exclusive of costs. Wyo. Stat. Ann. § 5-9-128. A damages claim exceeding that amount would need to be pursued separately in district court. Notably, § 1-21-1017 permits a business entity to appear and litigate a forcible entry and detainer action pro se — without an attorney — through an owner, shareholder, member, or partner, provided the entity gives written notice of this representation to the court and all parties; if an attorney later appears for the entity, the opposing party is entitled to a continuance to obtain its own counsel.

sections.heading: Timing
sections.text: After the complaint is filed and served, the court must set a hearing within twelve days, and the tenant must be served with the complaint and summons no less than three and no more than twelve days before trial. Id. § 1-21-1004. Once judgment is entered, the landlord may obtain a writ of restitution directing the sheriff to restore possession; absent an appeal, the writ must be executed within two days of receipt (Sundays excepted). Id. § 1-21-1013.

sections.heading: Damages
sections.text: Acceleration-of-rent clauses are enforceable in Wyoming, and there is no statute requiring a landlord to mitigate damages following a commercial tenant's default.

sections.heading: Special Considerations
sections.text: Trial may be before the judge or a jury. Id. § 1-21-1008–1010. A losing tenant has thirty days to appeal, but an appeal does not stay enforcement of the judgment unless, within forty-eight hours after judgment (Sundays excepted), the appellant files a bond with two or more sufficient sureties, conditioned on payment of accrued and future costs and damages sustained by the plaintiff from the wrongful detention during the appeal. Id. § 1-21-1004, 1-21-1014. As noted above, § 1-21-1017 (enacted 2021) allows a non-attorney owner, member, or partner to represent a business-entity landlord or tenant in an FED proceeding — a practical, cost-saving option not available in ordinary civil litigation.

leaseConsiderations: Express acceleration clause, enforceable under Wyoming law and useful given the absence of a statutory mitigation duty.
No-mitigation acknowledgment or, alternatively, an express mitigation obligation if the parties prefer to allocate that risk contractually.
Contractual notice periods, since the three-day statutory notice is a floor that parties may lengthen (but generally not shorten) by agreement.
Attorney's fees provision, since Wyoming does not provide a general statutory right to fees in commercial FED actions.
Self-help caution clause specifying any agreed peaceable-reentry procedure, given the absence of a controlling statute or case law on commercial self-help.
Appeal-bond awareness — confirm lease remedies and holdover damages language anticipate the forty-eight-hour bond deadline that governs whether a tenant's appeal stays enforcement.
Entity-representation planning — if the landlord is an LLC or similar entity, note the § 1-21-1017 option for an owner/member to litigate FED actions without counsel.
Jurisdictional-limit awareness — structure or bifurcate damages claims exceeding $50,000 for filing in district court rather than assuming joinder with the circuit court possession action.

Ann. § 5-9-128 (circuit court general civil jurisdiction, $50,000 threshold). The $7,000 jurisdictional figure in the 2022 baseline is corrected here; Wyoming's circuit court general civil jurisdiction has stood at $50,000 since a 2011 statutory increase, and no 2023–2026 amendment to that threshold or to Article 10's core notice/timing provisions was identified in this research.
